questions.title: An orchestrator sets a $2.00 limit per user request, yet allows spawning sub-agents with an independent $2.00 cap each up to depth 3 (1 root orchestrator spawns 3 level-1 sub-agents, and each level-1 spawns 3 level-2 sub-agents). What is the worst-case spend for one request if caps are not shared?
questions.context: Count the root orchestrator plus all spawned level-1 and level-2 sub-agents, assuming each exhausts its $2.00 limit.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: The hierarchy contains 1 (root) + 3 (level-1) + (3 × 3 = 9 level-2) = 13 active agents; with unshared $2.00 local limits, worst-case spend is 13 × $2.00 = **$26** (13× the intended cap). Without a shared trace-scoped budget ledger, delegating subtasks multiplies allowances exponentially by branching factor and depth. A stuck planning tree where workers recursively delegate subtasks to fresh sub-agents silently blows past org spending limits within minutes. Enforcing one atomic `BudgetLedger` keyed by root `trace_id` (plus reserving estimated spend before parallel dispatch) bounds total spend strictly, at the cost of gracefully aborting incomplete leaf branches when shared allowance hits zero.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Your single-agent coding loop ends every edit by prompting itself "Double-check that your patch satisfies all edge cases and tests pass." Logs show it approves 96% of its own broken patches without running `pytest`. Why, and what fixes it?
questions.context: The agent has a `run_tests` tool available, and the harness accepts verbal completion without checking test exit codes.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Autoregressive confirmation bias makes a generator model trust its own recent patch trajectory, while missing deterministic harness gates allow verbal claims to bypass verification. Attention over the model's preceding edits biases the next tokens toward `"Everything is sound"`, and assistant post-training rewards confident closure rather than calling a slow test runner. Accepting self-attestation ships 96% of broken patches straight to code review. Enforcing a deterministic verification gate (blocking completion until linting and `pytest` return exit code 0) paired with an isolated **Maker-Checker** Evaluator spinning up in a fresh context on only the `git diff` and spec eliminates sycophancy at the cost of extra test runtime and 1–2 checker calls.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Design a bounded-autonomy approval flow for an enterprise infrastructure agent that proposes Terraform changes, waits up to 24 hours for human sign-off, and guarantees the approved plan matches what executes.
questions.context: Cloud state can drift during the 24-hour wait; workers must not hold idle containers or locks overnight.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Persist durable workflow checkpoints and bind human approval to a cryptographic hash of the exact serialized Terraform plan before releasing worker compute. First, the agent generates the plan inside a read-only sandbox, saves the plan binary plus its `SHA-256` digest and structured resource-change summary, and yields cleanly into `AWAITING_APPROVAL`. Second, the approval token records `(trace_id, plan_sha256, approver_id, expiry)`. Third, on resume within 24 hours, a stateless worker verifies the signature, checks `plan_sha256`, confirms zero state drift against live infrastructure, and applies via scoped credentials. Re-running `terraform plan` after approval without hash verification risks executing unreviewed deletions caused by concurrent drift, while hash-bound checkpoints drop idle compute to zero at the cost of requiring re-approval if state drifts.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Your agent connects to third-party MCP tool servers to read tickets and update Jira. How do you enforce bounded autonomy against rug-pull tool description updates, oversized tool outputs, and argument injection?
questions.context: External MCP servers can mutate metadata over time; tool outputs can reach 100k tokens containing user-submitted HTML.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Treat third-party MCP servers as untrusted dependencies: pin tool schemas by hash, cap and delimit returned payloads, and enforce RBAC and policy checks outside the model before execution. First, compute and pin `SHA-256` digests of approved tool names, descriptions, and JSON Schemas—halting and alerting if a server silently modifies descriptions ("tool-poisoning rug pull"). Second, truncate tool responses to strict byte limits, strip invisible formatting or HTML tags, and wrap text in untrusted-data markers. Third, validate Jira project and ticket IDs against the caller's actual RBAC scope before executing mutations. Without schema pinning and RBAC checks, a mutated tool description can trick the agent into copying private tickets into public comments, trading manual approval on server updates for strong supply-chain containment.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: A healthcare chatbot runs a PII redaction guardrail only on the LLM's output before showing text to the patient. Why is relying solely on an output guardrail insufficient when calling a third-party model API?
questions.context: Patients paste names, SSNs, and lab values into chat messages; the LLM runs on an external hosted API.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Running PII redaction only on outputs lets raw patient identifiers cross the external trust boundary on every inbound API request. Input guardrails operate inside your VPC before calling external models—detecting and replacing SSNs, names, or keys with reversible tokens (`<SSN_1>`) or blocking banned payloads—while output guardrails validate generated text for policy compliance, grounding, and leakage before rendering to users. Even if an output filter scrubs an echoed SSN, transmitting the raw prompt externally already violates data-minimization and HIPAA logging boundaries, and models can paraphrase sensitive facts past simple output regexes. Pre-model PII tokenization keeps raw secrets local at the cost of ~10–40 ms added TTFT and occasional over-masking of benign numeric IDs.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Raw PII has already crossed the trust boundary to the external provider (and its telemetry) before output filtering runs, and paraphrases can slip past output checks.
options.why: Masking or tokenizing sensitive fields in an input guardrail inside your VPC keeps raw PII out of third-party requests.

options.text: Output guardrails increase the LLM's input token bill.
options.why: Output checks run after generation and do not change input token counts.

options.text: Output guardrails cannot catch any prompt injection, whereas input regexes catch 100% of attacks.
options.why: No regex catches 100% of prompt injections; the primary exposure here is sending raw PII outbound.

options.text: Input guardrails make model weights forget memorized training data.
options.why: Runtime guardrails filter traffic at inference boundaries and never modify model weights.

questions.title: Your input safety guardrail achieves 99% recall on prompt attacks and a 4% false-positive rate on normal support queries. Why is this a severe product bug, and how do you measure and tune it?
questions.context: The support bot serves 50,000 customer messages daily, of which roughly 99% are benign questions.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Because benign queries vastly outnumber attacks, a 4% false-positive rate blocks roughly 1,980 legitimate paying customers every day, turning safety tuning into a major availability outage. Guardrail classifiers trade recall against false refusals via threshold calibration, and balanced lab test sets hide how severely the benign base rate multiplies false positives in production. A rigid keyword or over-sensitive jailbreak classifier rejects normal requests like `"how do I kill a stalled background job?"` or `"ignore my previous invoice"`. Build a dedicated benign-adversarial eval slice (safe queries using trigger words) alongside attack suites, raise the hard-block threshold to keep false refusals under 0.5%, and route medium-risk scores to strict-mode prompts rather than instant blocks—trading tiny recall margin for customer usability.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: A financial assistant serves 200,000 requests/day. Real attacks are 0.5% of traffic (1,000 requests) and benign traffic is 99.5% (199,000 requests). Your input guardrail achieves 95% true-positive rate on attacks and a 2% false-positive rate on benign queries. How many benign user requests are wrongly blocked per day?
questions.context: Compute the daily blocked benign count directly from the 199,000 benign base.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: 199,000 benign requests/day × 0.02 false-positive rate = **3,980 wrongly blocked benign requests per day** (more than 4× the 950 real attacks caught!). Under a 199:1 benign-to-attack base rate, the positive predictive value of a guardrail block is only 950 ÷ (950 + 3,980) ≈ 19.3%, meaning four out of five blocked users are legitimate customers. Calibrating guardrail thresholds on 50/50 balanced test sets misses this base-rate collapse completely. Routing medium-confidence flags through a second-stage verifier or safer degraded prompt cuts customer lockouts dramatically at the cost of added latency on the ~2.5% flagged slice.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: During a traffic spike, your external guardrail classifier starts timing out after 500 ms. A developer sets `fail_open: true` globally on the API gateway. What fails in production, and when is `fail_open` the wrong default?
questions.context: The gateway serves both a public marketing FAQ bot and an internal medical-records assistant.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Global `fail_open: true` silently strips all PII and policy enforcement whenever the guardrail service slows down, giving attackers a trivial timeout-based bypass on sensitive routes. Gateways should apply risk-tiered policies: **fail-closed** (returning a safe fallback error or queuing) on regulated, PII-bearing, and tool-executing paths like medical records, while allowing bounded fail-open (backed by fast local regex checks plus async audit logging) only on low-risk public FAQ endpoints. During a traffic surge under global fail-open, raw patient data and unscreened tool calls flow unchecked for the entire outage window. Risk-tiered fail-closed defaults preserve compliance boundaries at the cost of partial service degradation (`503`) during upstream classifier outages.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Fail-open rejects all requests immediately with HTTP 503.
options.why: Rejecting on dependency timeouts is fail-closed; fail-open lets traffic proceed without the check.

options.text: Fail-open doubles the LLM's output token limit.
options.why: Skipping a timed-out guardrail does not alter generation parameters.

options.text: Fail-open exposes guardrail model weights in error headers.
options.why: Timeouts bypass evaluation; they never serialize model parameters.

options.text: Fail-open disables safety and PII enforcement under overload, allowing attackers to force unguarded LLM calls by stalling the guardrail.
options.why: On regulated endpoints like medical records, timeouts turn into an intentional policy-bypass vulnerability.

questions.title: Why do output guardrails conflict with low-latency token streaming, and how do production gateways resolve that tension without buffering the entire response?
questions.context: Users expect first tokens under 400 ms; a 500-token response takes 6 seconds to finish while an output filter checks PII and policy.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Waiting for complete responses to run output classifiers inflates TTFT from 300 ms to 6 seconds, while flushing every single token immediately exposes banned text or split PII before checks finish. Production gateways use **sliding micro-window buffering**: hold back small chunks (roughly 20–40 tokens or sentence boundaries, adding ~150–250 ms), execute fast deterministic PII/regex scanners synchronously and rolling-context classifiers per window before flushing to the SSE stream, and immediately terminate and replace the client bubble if a violation fires mid-stream. Flushing tokens raw lets half a credit card number appear on screen for seconds before post-hoc deletion. Micro-window buffering preserves sub-500 ms streaming feel while catching token-boundary leaks at the cost of slightly chunkier UI updates.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: A system guards against indirect prompt injection using three independent defense layers: input delimiter plus classifier (catches 70% of attacks), tool-argument validator (catches 80% of remaining), and outbound domain allowlist (catches 90% of remaining). What percentage of attacks succeed past all three layers? (One decimal.)
questions.context: Assume each layer acts independently on attacks surviving earlier layers.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Survival rates multiply across independent layers: (1 − 0.70) × (1 − 0.80) × (1 − 0.90) = 0.30 × 0.20 × 0.10 = 0.006 = **0.6%** attack pass-through (99.4% blocked). Combining heterogeneous layers across distinct trust boundaries—semantic text classifiers, deterministic schema/value validators, and network allowlists—prevents any single evasion trick from compromising the application. In practice, if two layers rely on the same LLM family or shared regex list, failures correlate strongly so an encoding bypass fools both layers simultaneously. Orthogonal defense in depth drives residual bypass rates below 1% at the cost of ~30–80 ms cumulative gateway latency and maintaining rules at each boundary.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: A new prompt and guardrail update rolls out as a 5% canary on 80,000 uniform daily requests, checked every 15-minute window before auto-rollback triggers. If a bug causes 12% of canary responses to emit unsafe text, how many unsafe responses occur in one 15-minute window before rollback?
questions.context: Assume uniform traffic across 24 hours (96 windows of 15 minutes per day).
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: 80,000 requests/day ÷ 96 windows/day = 833.33 requests per 15-minute window; 5% canary share = 41.67 canary requests; 12% defect rate × 41.67 = **5 unsafe responses** per 15-minute window (versus 100 unsafe responses at 100% traffic). Canary rollouts bound blast radius (`traffic_share × window_volume × defect_rate`) while gathering enough events to trigger automated rollback on safety regressions. Sizing a canary too small (0.1%, under 1 event per window) delays anomaly detection for hours, whereas skipping staged rollouts exposes 20× more users immediately. Automated safety canaries limit user harm at the cost of slower deployment velocity and maintaining segmented telemetry pipelines.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Your input guardrail blocks exact banned phrases and regex PII patterns cleanly in unit tests, yet red-teamers bypass it using zero-width spaces, base64 strings, or visually identical Cyrillic letters (`а` for `a`). Why, and what fixes the mismatch?
questions.context: The LLM executes the obfuscated instructions easily while the regex guardrail reports zero matches.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Parser mismatch happens when deterministic guardrails scan raw byte strings while LLMs generalize across homoglyphs, invisible codepoints, and base64 encodings. Apply deterministic input sanitization before rules evaluate: Unicode NFKC normalization, stripping zero-width joiners and bidi-override characters, collapsing odd whitespace, and flagging or decoding unexpected base64/hex payloads—paired with semantic classifiers trained on adversarial paraphrases. Inserting one U+200B character inside `"ignore previous instructions"` skips literal regex rules while the LLM obeys it without trouble. Aggressive normalization shuts down naive evasion cleanly, at the cost of careful exemptions for legitimate multilingual content or valid developer code payloads containing encodings.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Switch from Python `re` to Rust regex for faster matching.
options.why: Regex engine speed does not resolve invisible Unicode characters, homoglyphs, or base64 encoding.

options.text: Truncate incoming user prompts to 100 characters.
options.why: Short obfuscated attacks still fit inside 100 characters while legitimate queries break.

options.text: Normalize text (Unicode NFKC, strip zero-width/bidi controls, decode or flag obfuscated encodings) before deterministic rules run, paired with semantic classifiers.
options.why: Because modern tokenizers map obfuscated variants toward the same semantics, guardrails must inspect the normalized representation.

options.text: Lower the LLM's temperature to 0.
options.why: Temperature adjusts sampling randomness and does not stop the model from following obfuscated prompt instructions.

questions.title: When an output guardrail fires in production, returning a blunt `"I cannot help with that"` breaks downstream callers or leaks which rule triggered. Compare the four response policies when a guardrail triggers and when to use each.
questions.context: Your gateway serves consumer chat, strict JSON extraction APIs, and internal support agents.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Match the trigger action to caller contract and risk level across four policies: (1) **In-place redaction** (mask detected PII/tokens while keeping safe prose—best for partial leaks in otherwise valid answers); (2) **Constrained regeneration** (retry once with violation feedback or escalate to a stricter model—best for recoverable tone or citation slips); (3) **Neutral fallback message** (return a helpful domain redirect without echoing the exact triggered rule—best for consumer chat); (4) **Structured error payload plus escalation** (emit valid schema `{blocked: true, reason_code}` and log an alert—mandatory for programmatic APIs and compliance triggers). Returning plain refusal prose on a JSON endpoint crashes callers, while verbose rule explanations become probing oracles for attackers. Tiered actions preserve contracts and security at the cost of maintaining fallback paths.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: After enabling a strict faithfulness/grounding guardrail on a RAG assistant, useful answers drop 22% because the guardrail flags harmless connective reasoning ("Because your plan renewed in March...") as unsupported hallucinations. How do you debug and recalibrate this?
questions.context: The guardrail runs `all_claims_supported` using a small NLI classifier; user satisfaction fell sharply post-launch.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Slice blocked traces by failure mode to separate true fabrications from cross-chunk synthesis and minor date/math inferences, then adjust NLI scope and enforcement policy. Small NLI models score `"neutral"` when an answer combines facts across two separate chunks or derives simple arithmetic (`"March + 30 days"`), causing hard blocks when evaluated chunk-by-chunk. Evaluating claims against the concatenated retrieved context, separating verifiable factual claims (amounts, dates, names) from connective prose, and switching uncertain claims from full deletion to inline source citations or soft caution tags recovers the lost 22% utility. Hard-blocking every NLI neutral score destroys helpfulness, while soft-flagging plus citation checks trades minor unverified prose risk for reliable user answers.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Design a guardrail pipeline for a high-throughput enterprise assistant with a strict 150 ms guardrail latency budget, where full LLM-as-judge checks take 700 ms synchronously.
questions.context: Traffic is 1,000 QPS; 35% of queries are benign FAQs, while 5% trigger sensitive write tools.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Split guardrails into a sub-150 ms synchronous fast-path and conditional/asynchronous deep evaluation reserved for uncertain or high-risk requests. On every request, run parallel checks under 40 ms: text normalization, deterministic regex/allowlist rules, and lightweight quantized encoder classifiers (safety + PII NER). Invoke the 700 ms deep judge synchronously *only* when the fast classifier scores in an ambiguous band or before the 5% of requests executing sensitive write tools; run deep hallucination/compliance judges asynchronously on sampled read-only logs to drive alerts and daily threshold updates. Running a 700 ms judge synchronously on all 1,000 QPS breaches every latency SLO and doubles GPU cost, while tiered gating hits budget on 95% of traffic at the cost of post-hoc detection on subtle read-only misses.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Red-teamers bypass your single-turn input guardrail by spreading a prohibited request across six innocent-looking conversation turns. How do you design stateful guardrails without blowing latency or context limits?
questions.context: Conversations reach 30 turns; current filters inspect only the newest user message.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Evaluate a compact rolling conversation risk state alongside recent turns instead of scanning only `messages[-1]` or feeding full 30-turn logs into heavy classifiers on every request. Store per-session state containing a cumulative risk score (with slow decay), count of prior borderline flags, and a concise 150-token rolling intent summary updated asynchronously; on each turn, classify `[intent_summary + last 2-3 turns]` inside ~250 tokens, and inspect accumulated model outputs too since partial earlier compliance weakens later refusals. Scanning only the newest message lets turn 6 (`"Now adapt those steps for target X"`) slip past innocently after turns 1–5 built the scaffold. Stateful rolling risk triggers progressive friction (disabling tools before hard blocking), trading minimal session state for multi-turn defense without locking out long benign chats.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: When a model generates tokens one at a time for a single user, what limits its speed on a GPU?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
**Prefill** processes the whole prompt in parallel: big matrix multiplications, compute-bound. **Decode** produces one token per forward pass: for each token the GPU streams every weight through for a few operations each, so it's **memory-bandwidth-bound**. That's why batching many users together makes decode far more efficient: the weights are read once per step and used for every sequence in the batch.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **So what improves single-user decode speed?** Moving fewer bytes per token: quantised weights, speculative decoding (several tokens per weight read), or hardware with more bandwidth.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Network latency between the user and the server.
options.why: That adds time before and after, not to each token's generation.

options.text: Compute: the GPU's FLOPs.
options.why: That's what limits prefill, where many tokens are processed in parallel.

options.text: Memory bandwidth: every new token has to read all the weights from GPU memory.
options.why: Decode does little arithmetic per byte it reads, so it waits on memory.

options.text: The tokenizer.
options.why: Tokenising is tiny compared with a forward pass.

questions.title: A 7B model in bf16 (14 GB of weights) runs on a GPU with 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth. What's the theoretical maximum decode speed for one sequence? (Tokens per second.)
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Each token reads every weight once: 2 × 10¹² bytes/s ÷ 14 × 10⁹ bytes = **143 tokens/s**. Real numbers land lower (the KV cache is read too, and kernels don't hit peak bandwidth), but this ceiling is the right first estimate, and it's why 7B models feel fast and 70B ones don't.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **What happens to this ceiling with a batch of 32?** Total throughput rises almost 32× until compute or KV-cache reads take over, because the weights are read once for all 32 sequences.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Same GPU, same model, but quantised to int4 weights (3.5 GB). What's the new ceiling for one sequence?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
2 × 10¹² ÷ 3.5 × 10⁹ = **571 tokens/s**, four times the bf16 figure, because decode speed follows the bytes moved. Quantisation is mainly a memory-bandwidth optimisation for decode, which is why weight-only quantisation is so common in serving.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **What does int4 cost you?** Some quality, and how much varies by model and task, so evaluate on your own prompts. Some kernels also dequantise on the fly and lose part of the speed-up.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: With 32 layers, 8 KV heads of dimension 128, and bf16 (2 bytes), how much KV cache does one token take? (KiB.)
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Each layer stores a key and a value for each KV head: 2 × 32 layers × 8 heads × 128 dims × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = **128 KiB** per token. With full multi-head attention (32 KV heads) it would be 512 KiB. Grouped-query attention cuts the cache by 4× here.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **Why doesn't the number of query heads appear?** Queries are used and thrown away each step. Only keys and values are cached for future tokens.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: How much KV cache does one sequence with an 8,192-token context need? (GiB.)
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
8,192 tokens × 128 KiB = 1,048,576 KiB = **1 GiB** per sequence. Long contexts are expensive mainly because of the cache, not the weights.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **And at 128k context?** 16 GiB for a single sequence, more than the 7B model's weights.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: After loading the weights, 40 GiB of GPU memory is left for the KV cache. How many 8k-token sequences can run at once?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
40 GiB ÷ 1 GiB per sequence = **40** sequences. This is what really limits how many users one GPU can serve. It's why paged attention (allocating the cache in small blocks as sequences grow, instead of reserving the maximum up front) raises throughput so much: most sequences never reach 8k.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **How else can you fit more?** Quantise the KV cache to 8 bits (twice the sequences), cap the context length, or use a model with fewer KV heads.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Why do most recent open models use grouped-query attention (GQA)?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
In decode, every step reads the whole KV cache. **GQA** lets groups of query heads share one key-value head, so the cache and the bandwidth it needs shrink by the group factor. Multi-query attention (one KV head) is the extreme case and costs more quality.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **Can you convert a multi-head model to GQA?** Yes, by averaging the key and value heads in each group and then continuing training for a while (uptraining), as in the original GQA paper.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: It improves accuracy over multi-head attention.
options.why: It's chosen for efficiency, at a small cost in quality, or about the same quality.

options.text: Several query heads share each key-value head, which shrinks the KV cache and the memory read per token.
options.why: With 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, the cache is 4× smaller.

options.text: It increases the context length.
options.why: It makes long contexts cheaper, but it doesn't change the maximum by itself.

options.text: It makes training faster.
options.why: The main benefit is at inference, through the cache.

questions.title: With static batching, a batch of 16 requests finishes only when the longest answer finishes. What does continuous batching change?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Output lengths vary widely. In static batching, a request that finishes early holds an empty slot until the longest one ends. **Continuous (in-flight) batching** schedules per decode step: it evicts finished sequences and inserts new ones straight away. Combined with paged KV caches, it's the main reason modern serving engines get several times more throughput from the same GPU.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **What's the cost?** More complex scheduling and memory management, and prefill for new requests competes with decode for existing ones, which is why engines offer chunked prefill.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Finished sequences leave the batch at every step and waiting requests join, so slots never sit idle.
options.why: It's scheduling at the token step, not at the request.

options.text: It processes requests one at a time.
options.why: That's the opposite: no batching at all.

options.text: It makes each forward pass faster.
options.why: A step costs about the same. More of each step's work is useful.

options.text: It compresses the KV cache.
options.why: That's a separate optimisation.

questions.title: Users say answers take a long time to *start*, but once text appears it streams quickly. Which metric is bad, and what are the usual fixes?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
TTFT covers queueing plus prefill of the whole prompt. Long system prompts and retrieved context make prefill slow. Fixes: **prefix caching** (keep the KV cache of a shared system prompt and reuse it), trimming retrieved context, **chunked prefill** so long prompts don't block everyone, and enough capacity that requests don't queue. Report TTFT and time per output token separately. They have different causes.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **How would you measure where TTFT goes?** Log the queue wait, prefill time and prompt length per request, then plot TTFT against prompt length.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Throughput: add more GPUs.
options.why: More GPUs can help with queueing, but the specific symptom is the delay before the first token.

options.text: Time to first token (TTFT): reuse shared prompt prefixes, shorten prompts, and reduce queueing.
options.why: Streaming speed (time per output token) is fine here.

options.text: Time per output token: quantise the model.
options.why: That's the metric users say is fine.

options.text: Accuracy: fine-tune the model.
options.why: Quality isn't the complaint.

questions.title: Every request starts with the same 3,000-token system prompt. Which optimisation targets that directly?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Prefill for 3,000 identical tokens on every request is pure waste. **Prefix caching** stores the KV blocks for a common prefix and maps new requests onto them, cutting TTFT and compute. Many API providers bill cached input tokens at a discount for the same reason. Put the stable parts of the prompt first and the variable parts last, so the shared prefix stays as long as possible.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **What breaks prefix caching?** Anything that changes early tokens: a timestamp or user name at the top of the system prompt invalidates the cache for everything after it.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Quantising the KV cache.
options.why: That saves memory but still recomputes the prefix every time.

options.text: Prefix (prompt) caching: compute the KV cache for the shared prefix once and reuse it.
options.why: Requests skip prefill for the shared part.

options.text: Speculative decoding.
options.why: That speeds up generating the output, not processing the prompt.

options.text: Increasing temperature.
options.why: Temperature changes sampling, not the cost.

questions.title: In speculative decoding, a small draft model proposes 4 tokens and the large model checks them in one pass. Each draft token is accepted with probability 0.8, independently, and checking stops at the first rejection. On average, how many tokens does each pass of the large model produce? (Two decimals.)
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
The large model always produces at least one token (its own correction or continuation), plus each accepted draft token. The expected count is (1 − α^(k+1)) ÷ (1 − α) = (1 − 0.8⁵) ÷ 0.2 = **3.36** tokens per pass of the large model. Decode is memory-bound, so checking 4 tokens costs about the same as producing 1. That's where the speed-up comes from: about 3.4× fewer large-model passes, minus the draft model's own cost.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **When does speculative decoding not help?** When acceptance is low (the draft model predicts the large one poorly), or when the server is already compute-bound from large batches.
- **Does it change the output?** No. With the standard acceptance rule, outputs come from the large model's distribution exactly.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: With temperature 0 in production, the same prompt sometimes gets slightly different answers. What's the usual explanation?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Greedy decoding picks the highest-probability token, but the logits themselves vary by tiny amounts depending on **which other requests share the batch**, because kernel choice and reduction order change. When two tokens are nearly tied, that's enough to flip the choice, and the rest of the text diverges from there. Batch-invariant kernels can make serving fully deterministic, at some cost in speed.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **Why does this matter for evaluation?** A single run of an eval set is a sample. Run it more than once, or accept a margin, before calling a 1-point change real.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: The model has a bug.
options.why: This happens with correct models and serving engines.

options.text: Temperature 0 still samples randomly.
options.why: At temperature 0, decoding takes the argmax, with no sampling.

options.text: The tokenizer is non-deterministic.
options.why: Tokenisation is deterministic.

options.text: Floating-point results depend on how requests are batched together, so tiny numerical differences can change which token wins a near-tie.
options.why: Batch composition changes the order of the GPU's reductions, and floating-point addition isn't associative.

questions.title: A support bot must answer from a policy manual that changes every week. Fine-tune, or use RAG?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Rule of thumb: **RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behaviour.** Retrieval keeps facts current and lets answers cite their source. Fine-tuning is good at teaching a format, a tone, a task-specific skill, or shortening prompts, and much less reliable at teaching facts. Many production systems use both: a lightly fine-tuned model that's good at answering from retrieved documents.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **When would you fine-tune here?** If the bot keeps ignoring the output format, or needs to follow a complex escalation procedure more reliably than prompting achieves.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Fine-tune once, then never update.
options.why: The bot would be out of date within a week.

options.text: Fine-tune every week on the new manual.
options.why: Expensive, slow to update, and fine-tuning is unreliable at teaching facts precisely.

options.text: Neither: write a longer system prompt with the whole manual.
options.why: That works for a short manual. Retrieval scales further and keeps prompts short.

options.text: RAG: put the current policy in the context at query time.
options.why: Knowledge that changes weekly belongs in retrieval, not in the weights.

questions.title: What does LoRA train?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
For a weight matrix W (d × d), LoRA learns B (d × r) and A (r × d) with r much smaller than d, and uses W + (α/r)·BA in the forward pass. Only A and B get gradients and optimiser state, so memory and checkpoint size drop sharply. The adapter can be merged into W after training, so inference costs nothing extra, or kept separate and swapped per customer.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **Which matrices do people usually adapt?** The attention projections, and increasingly the MLP projections too. Adapting more matrices usually helps quality more than raising the rank does.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: All the weights, at a lower learning rate.
options.why: That's full fine-tuning.

options.text: Only the final classification layer.
options.why: That's linear probing or head-only training.

options.text: Two small low-rank matrices per adapted weight matrix. Their product is added to the frozen original weights.
options.why: W stays frozen, and only A and B (rank r) are trained.

options.text: A new set of embeddings for special tokens only.
options.why: That's closer to prompt tuning.

questions.title: LoRA with rank 16 on one 4,096 × 4,096 projection matrix. How many trainable parameters does that add?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
A is 16 × 4,096 and B is 4,096 × 16: 2 × 4,096 × 16 = **131,072** parameters, against 16,777,216 in the matrix itself.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **Why does such a small adapter work?** Fine-tuning updates tend to have low intrinsic rank: the change a task needs can be expressed in a few directions.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: As a percentage of that matrix's 16,777,216 parameters, how many does the rank-16 adapter train? (Percent, three decimals.)
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
131,072 ÷ 16,777,216 × 100 = **0.781%**. Across a whole model, LoRA typically trains 0.1–1% of the parameters. Optimiser state shrinks by the same factor, which is what makes a single-GPU fine-tune possible.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **Does fewer trainable parameters mean worse results?** For adapting style and task format, LoRA is usually close to full fine-tuning. For teaching a lot of new capability, full fine-tuning tends to win.
