Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
QLoRA quantises the frozen base weights to 4-bit NormalFloat, dequantises them on the fly in the forward pass, and backpropagates into bf16 LoRA adapters. Paged optimisers handle memory spikes. A 7B model's base weights take about 3.5 GB instead of 14 GB, so fine-tuning fits on one consumer GPU.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **What's the trade-off?** Slower steps, from dequantising, and a small quality gap that's usually negligible for instruction tuning.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: It quantises the adapters to 4-bit.
options.why: The adapters stay in bf16 or fp16. Only the frozen base is 4-bit.

options.text: It removes the need for a GPU.
options.why: It reduces memory a lot, but training still needs a GPU.

options.text: It trains a smaller model and then distils it.
options.why: That's distillation, a different technique.

options.text: The frozen base model is stored in 4-bit, while the LoRA adapters train in higher precision.
options.why: The base model's memory drops about 4× compared with bf16.

questions.title: You fine-tune on 10,000 examples averaging 1,500 tokens each, for 3 epochs. How many training tokens is that, in millions?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
10,000 × 1,500 × 3 = 45,000,000 = **45 million** tokens. It's the number that sets both the cost (hosted fine-tuning is usually priced per training token) and the time (divide by your tokens per second).

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **Is 3 epochs a good default?** For small curated datasets, 1–3 is typical. Watch held-out task performance, because more epochs on small data overfits quickly.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: After fine-tuning on 5,000 legal Q&A pairs, the model is great at legal questions but worse at general instructions and basic maths. What happened, and what helps?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Training only on one narrow distribution overwrites general behaviour. Mitigations: **replay** (mix in 10–30% general instruction data), a smaller learning rate and fewer epochs, parameter-efficient methods like LoRA, which change fewer weights, and an eval suite that includes general tasks, so you notice the regression before shipping.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **How would you detect it before launch?** Run a fixed general-capability eval before and after every fine-tune, alongside the task eval.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Use a higher learning rate to finish faster.
options.why: Higher learning rates usually make forgetting worse.

options.text: The model was too small.
options.why: Larger models forget less, but the cause is the narrow training.

options.text: Catastrophic forgetting. Mix general instruction data back in, lower the learning rate or epochs, or use LoRA.
options.why: Narrow training pulls the weights away from what made the model generally capable.

options.text: The legal data must contain wrong maths.
options.why: It doesn't need to. Simply never seeing general tasks is enough.

questions.title: Validation loss on your fine-tuning data keeps going down, but when people try the model, its answers are getting worse. What's the likely gap?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Validation loss uses teacher forcing: the model always sees the correct previous tokens. At inference it builds on its own outputs, and small errors compound. Lower loss can also come from learning the references' phrasing, without getting better at the task. Evaluate **generated** outputs on held-out prompts, with task metrics, human review, or a validated judge, and choose checkpoints by that.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **Which checkpoint do you ship?** The one with the best generated-output eval, which is often earlier than the lowest validation loss.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: The tokenizer changed.
options.why: That would usually break loss too.

options.text: Validation loss scores the next token on reference answers, which isn't the same as the quality of the model's own generated answers. Evaluate on generated outputs.
options.why: Loss measures imitating the references token by token, not how good the model's own answers are.

options.text: The model needs more epochs.
options.why: More epochs would push the loss lower and may make generations worse still.

options.text: The validation set is too small.
options.why: Possible, but loss going down while generations get worse is a mismatch of metric, not only of sample size.

questions.title: A fine-tuned chat model works in your training notebook but produces rambling text when served. What do you check first?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Chat models learn a precise format: role markers, special tokens, and an end-of-turn token. If the server's template differs, even by a missing end-of-turn token or a different system-prompt marker, the model sees an unfamiliar format and doesn't know where its turn ends. Use the tokenizer's chat template in training and serving, and test the served endpoint with a prompt from the training set.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **What makes the model stop generating?** The end-of-turn or end-of-sequence token it was trained to produce. If serving doesn't treat that token as a stop, output runs on.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: That the server formats prompts with exactly the chat template and special tokens used in training.
options.why: A mismatched template is the most common cause of this.

options.text: The learning rate.
options.why: It works in the notebook, so training itself was probably fine.

options.text: The GPU type.
options.why: Hardware doesn't change the text like this.

options.text: Temperature.
options.why: Worth checking, but rambling that ignores turn structure points at the prompt format first.

questions.title: How does DPO differ from RLHF with PPO?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
RLHF with PPO trains a reward model on preference pairs, then optimises the policy with reinforcement learning against it, with a KL penalty to stay near the reference model: complex and finicky. **DPO** shows the same KL-constrained objective can be optimised directly, by raising the likelihood of the preferred answer relative to the rejected one (against the reference model). It's simpler and more stable, and widely used.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **What can go wrong with DPO?** It can overfit to the preference data and drift towards longer or more stylised answers. Watch length and held-out quality, and tune beta, which sets how far it can move from the reference.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: DPO only works for classification tasks.
options.why: It's used for aligning generative chat models.

options.text: DPO trains a bigger reward model.
options.why: DPO has no explicit reward model at all.

options.text: DPO learns directly from preference pairs with a classification-style loss, with no separate reward model and no reinforcement learning loop.
options.why: It optimises the same kind of preference objective in closed form.

options.text: DPO needs no preference data.
options.why: It needs pairs of preferred and rejected answers, the same data RLHF's reward model learns from.

questions.title: You can fine-tune on 1,000 examples carefully written by experts, or on 100,000 scraped Q&A pairs of mixed quality. For teaching an instruction-following style, which is usually better?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
For alignment-style tuning, the model already has the knowledge from pre-training. Fine-tuning mostly teaches the format and the manners. A small set of consistent, high-quality examples does that well, while large noisy sets teach inconsistency and errors. For teaching a genuinely new skill, you need more data, and quality still matters.

**Follow-ups you'll get**

- **How would you clean the 100,000?** Deduplicate, filter with heuristics and a quality classifier or judge, check a random sample by hand, and keep only what you'd be happy for the model to imitate.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: The 100,000 pairs, because more data always wins.
options.why: More data helps when it's good. Noisy examples teach noisy behaviour.

options.text: The 1,000 expert examples. For style and format, quality and consistency matter more than volume.
options.why: Small, carefully curated instruction sets have done surprisingly well (the LIMA result).

options.text: Neither. Fine-tuning can't change style.
options.why: Changing style and format is what fine-tuning is best at.

options.text: Mix them equally.
options.why: Mixing in mostly-noisy data dilutes the good examples.

questions.title: Your production extraction service calls the provider's floating `model-latest` alias rather than a pinned dated snapshot. Why is this risky even when API uptime is 100%?
questions.context: Downstream workflows expect deterministic JSON field formats and calibrated confidence thresholds measured in last month's evaluation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Floating aliases let the provider swap weights or system defaults underneath live traffic, silently invalidating your prompt tuning and calibrated thresholds. Every production endpoint should pin an immutable snapshot ID and treat a model upgrade like a code release: run shadow comparisons and regression evals on the candidate snapshot before shifting canary traffic. A routine silent update often alters whitespace formatting, tool-call verbosity, or borderline refusal rates overnight while HTTP 200 status codes stay green. Pinning guarantees behavioral reproducibility across incidents, at the cost of tracking deprecation dates and running scheduled migration gates before old snapshots retire.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Floating aliases double per-token billing without changing weights.
options.why: Provider aliases carry the same published token pricing as the underlying snapshot.

options.text: Aliases bypass prompt caching at the network edge.
options.why: Caching still works per prefix until the underlying weights change and invalidate KV compatibility.

options.text: Provider-side model updates silently shift output distributions, formatting habits, and safety refusals without any deploy on your side.
options.why: Pinning an immutable version keeps behavior frozen until you replay your regression suite on the new snapshot.

options.text: Floating aliases disable streaming responses.
options.why: Streaming transport works identically across pinned and unpinned model identifiers.

questions.title: When should you choose a specialized 8B model (or fine-tuned encoder) over a frontier reasoning model in a production system?
questions.context: A support router classifies 400 tickets/second into 12 fixed intents under a strict 150 ms p99 latency SLA.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Choose a specialized small model when the task has bounded input-output structure, tight latency or cost targets, and enough labeled examples to match frontier quality on that narrow distribution. Small encoders or distilled 8B models finish in tens of milliseconds on compact GPUs and avoid verbose reasoning drift on rigid schemas. Sending 400 classification requests per second to a frontier reasoning model blows latency budgets, multiplies spend by 10–30×, and introduces occasional explanatory prose around enum labels. Narrow models win on predictable unit economics and speed, trading away broad zero-shot generalization when new ticket categories emerge.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: A two-tier router serves 1,000,000 monthly requests averaging 1,000 input tokens and 300 output tokens each. It sends 70% of requests to a fast tier ($0.15/1M input, $0.60/1M output) and 30% to a frontier tier ($3.00/1M input, $15.00/1M output), while the router classifier adds $0.02 per 1,000 requests. What is the total monthly spend in USD?
questions.context: Assume no prompt caching discounts and zero retries across the 1,000,000 requests.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Compute each tier separately plus router overhead:

- **Fast tier (700,000 requests):** 700M input tokens × $0.15 = $105.00; 210M output tokens × $0.60 = $126.00; subtotal = $231.00.
- **Frontier tier (300,000 requests):** 300M input tokens × $3.00 = $900.00; 90M output tokens × $15.00 = $1,350.00; subtotal = $2,250.00.
- **Router overhead:** 1,000 thousand requests × $0.02 = $20.00.

Total spend is $231 + $2,250 + $20 = **$2,501**, saving two-thirds compared with sending all traffic to the frontier model ($7,500). Output tokens dominate the frontier bill ($1,350 vs $900), so routing verbose generation tasks accurately yields the biggest savings while misrouting easy verbose replies wastes budget fast.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Compare an upfront predictive router against a sequential confidence cascade. When does a cascade lose both latency and cost against direct frontier calls?
questions.context: User-facing coding assistant expects sub-second TTFT; complex multi-file queries make up 65% of live traffic.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: An upfront router classifies query difficulty before generation, whereas a sequential cascade tries the cheap model first, evaluates the draft, and escalates weak outputs to the frontier tier. When complex queries dominate traffic, cascades burn both time and money: 65% of users wait through a full small-model decode and verifier check only to restart from scratch on the frontier model. Under heavy escalation, streaming cannot begin safely until verification clears, destroying perceived TTFT. Upfront routing cuts tail latency when labeled routing data exists, trading verifier accuracy on ambiguous edge cases for single-hop dispatch.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: When the small model answers correctly 95% of the time without needing verification.
options.why: High small-model pass rates make sequential cascades maximally cheap because few requests escalate.

options.text: When most queries escalate to the frontier tier anyway, forcing requests to pay small-model generation plus verifier latency before starting the frontier call.
options.why: At high escalation rates, the cascade adds wasted small-model tokens and doubles first-token wait for the majority of users.

options.text: When the predictive router uses a logistic regression classifier over embeddings.
options.why: Lightweight embedding classifiers add under 10 ms overhead and avoid running any failed LLM generation first.

options.text: When frontier pricing is lower than small-model pricing.
options.why: Frontier models carry higher per-token costs; the issue is paying two generations plus verification on escalated traffic.

questions.title: Sending a request directly to a frontier model costs $0.020. A cascade instead runs a small model ($0.002) plus an external verifier ($0.002) on every request, then escalates failing cases to the frontier model ($0.020). What is the maximum escalation rate (in percent) where the cascade still stays cheaper than calling the frontier model directly?
questions.context: Ignore latency cost and assume all escalated requests pay both the initial cascade pass and the full frontier price.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Each request pays $0.002 + $0.002 = $0.004 upfront, plus `e × $0.020` for escalated traffic. Setting expected cost below direct frontier cost gives `0.004 + 0.020 × e < 0.020`, so `0.020 × e < 0.016`, yielding break-even escalation **`e = 80%`**. Beyond 80% escalation, paying the small model and verifier wastes more money than skipping straight to the frontier endpoint. In real systems where escalations also degrade TTFT and consume extra KV capacity, teams cap cascade escalation well below 40%–50% or switch to an upfront predictive router once traffic difficulty shifts upward.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Your two-tier cascade uses a small model with a prompt asking it to rate its own certainty (1–5) and escalates scores below 4. Monthly cost drops 55%, yet wrong answers on subtle policy edge cases jump while escalation stays at 12%. Why?
questions.context: Escalation rate sits near 12%, HTTP errors are zero, and customer complaints cluster around outdated exception rules.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Self-assessed confidence ratings from a small generator fail as a cascade gate because models hallucinate plausibly with high stated certainty (`5/5`). When subtle policy exceptions diverge from pretraining priors, the 8B model confidently outputs stale guidance and skips escalation, cutting API spend at the cost of silent accuracy collapse on the hardest 15% of queries. Production cascades replace self-ratings with external signals: deterministic schema or code checks, retrieval grounding scores, sequence log-probability margins, or an independent lightweight verifier model. External verifiers restore recall on policy traps at the cost of 20–100 ms verification overhead.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Small models are poorly calibrated on out-of-distribution errors and emit high self-confidence scores on fluent hallucinations.
options.why: Self-reported certainty correlates with surface fluency rather than factual accuracy on edge cases.

options.text: The frontier model is overriding small-model answers with lower quality.
options.why: Only 12% of queries ever reach the frontier tier, so the 88% handled by the small tier drives the accuracy drop.

options.text: Token-level log probabilities always return 1.0 under greedy decoding.
options.why: Greedy decoding picks the argmax token, whose softmax probability can still be low (for example 0.35), though prompted numeric self-ratings are even less calibrated.

options.text: Prompt caching hid the escalation instructions after the first request.
options.why: Prompt caching preserves exact prefix behavior and does not erase rubric instructions.

questions.title: On a 2,000-query golden benchmark, a tuned routing threshold sends 1,400 queries to the fast tier (where the fast tier achieves 88.0% accuracy) and 600 queries to the frontier tier (where the frontier tier achieves 95.0% accuracy). What is the router's blended accuracy in percent?
questions.context: Evaluate exact weighted accuracy across the 2,000 queries with no abstentions.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Count correct answers per slice: `(1,400 × 0.88) + (600 × 0.95) = 1,232 + 570 = 1,802` correct queries out of `2,000`, so blended accuracy is `1,802 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = ` **`90.1%`**. Tracking only aggregate accuracy can mislead if the 198 failures in the fast slice happen on high-stakes billing or medical intents. Reporting accuracy per routed bucket alongside cost-normalized accuracy shows whether the frontier tier would have fixed those 198 misses (avoidable routing errors) or whether both models failed on bad retrieval context, guiding threshold calibration vs data fixes.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: A chat coding assistant runs a per-turn router: greetings go to an 8B model and debugging turns go to a 70B model. Users report abrupt tone and formatting whiplash across turns, and provider prompt-cache hit rates sit near zero on long threads. What went wrong, and how do you fix it?
questions.context: Conversations average 8 turns; each turn re-sends the growing thread history.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Routing every turn independently breaks both behavioral continuity and prefix KV caching across a session. When turn 1 runs on an 8B model, turn 2 on a 70B model, and turn 3 back on an 8B model, neither provider holds warm prefix blocks from the prior turn (causing full prefill re-computation and zero cache discount), while the weaker model reads earlier 70B code blocks and regresses style or tool formatting mid-thread. Switch to **session-sticky routing** or a **one-way escalation ratchet**: classify the thread on turn 1, pin the session to that tier (or escalate permanently to the stronger model once complexity triggers), and keep the prefix immutable. Session pinning restores prompt-cache hits and tone stability at the cost of keeping escalated sessions on the pricier tier until reset.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Why do static leaderboard ranks (like overall MMLU or Arena Elo) fail as the sole model-selection criterion in an enterprise agent router, and what capability signals belong in the routing matrix instead?
questions.context: Your platform routes structured extraction, SQL tool-use, long-contract summarization, and non-English customer chat across four model families.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Aggregate benchmark averages mask steep per-capability cliffs—a model scoring top-3 on general chat can drop 25 points on parallel function calling, strict JSON grammar conformance, 64k-token multi-hop recall, or non-Latin tokenizer efficiency. Routing an enterprise SQL agent purely by Arena Elo sends complex multi-table joins to a chatty model that invents column names or breaks tool schemas under 40k context. Build a task-capability matrix from your own golden slices tracking schema pass rate, needle-reconciliation recall at real context lengths, non-English token fertility multiplier, and p99 TTFT. Capability-sliced routing matches workloads accurately at the cost of maintaining periodic eval runs per capability cell.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: You add a new fast model to a production semantic router. Aggregate p50 latency drops 30% and spend drops 25%, yet checkout conversion in French and German drops 14% with zero HTTP errors. How do you isolate and resolve this?
questions.context: English makes up 85% of daily queries; automated error-rate alerts remained silent.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Aggregate medians hid a localized quality regression because English traffic (85%) dominated global metrics while the new fast model degraded non-English prompts. Slice routing telemetry by `(model_id, locale, intent)` to compare refusal rates, output-token inflation, and conversion immediately before vs after router weights shifted. Often a fast model exhibits higher subword tokenization fertility on French/German—tripling token count toward `max_tokens` truncation—or overly aggressive safety refusals on translated idioms. Pin affected locales back to the baseline model, add per-locale minimum cohorts to automated canary gates, and require stratified multilingual evals before admitting new models, trading higher non-English token spend for preserved conversion.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Design a multi-region LLM routing gateway serving US, EU, and APAC users where EU prompts must stay strictly inside EU endpoints under data residency rules while minimizing global tail latency.
questions.context: Each region runs primary and secondary model endpoints; traffic peaks rotate across time zones.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Split routing into a hard **compliance filter** followed by a **region-local latency and health scorer**. First, bind tenant residency tags (`region_lock: eu`) in signed auth claims so the EU ingress router filters candidate endpoints exclusively to EU VPC clusters, hard-failing (`503`) rather than spilling over to US replicas during an EU outage. Second, within allowed regions, score healthy endpoints using EWMA TTFT, active queue depth, and circuit-breaker state; non-residency-locked APAC/US traffic can spill across nearest healthy neighbors when local GPUs saturate. Global health broadcasting without residency pinning risks silent cross-border PII transfers during failover. Hard policy filters plus local EWMA scoring maintain legal compliance and low latency at the cost of higher standby capacity inside locked regions.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Design an online contextual-bandit router that learns model selection weights from live production feedback without starving newly added models or chasing delayed labels blindly.
questions.context: Explicit feedback is rare; ticket resolution outcomes arrive 2 to 24 hours after a chat ends, and new models onboard monthly.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Use an off-policy logged contextual bandit (such as LinUCB or Thompson Sampling over query/task features) combined with bounded exploration (`epsilon = 2%–5%`), composite cost-quality rewards, and delayed attribution windows. Log the router's exact propensity score `p(arm | x)` at request time so delayed resolution signals arriving 24 hours later train updates without selection bias, while gating reward updates with short-horizon proxy checks (format validity, zero immediate re-asks) so catastrophic broken models halt within minutes instead of waiting 24 hours. Greedy argmax routing without exploration locks out newly onboarded models permanently, while uncapped exploration leaks bad answers to paying users. Propensity-logged shadow traffic plus capped exploration balances continual adaptation with strict user-experience bounds.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: When your primary frontier LLM times out on a RAG product-search assistant, what is the right graceful degradation order rather than immediately returning HTTP 500?
questions.context: Users are browsing product documentation; sub-second responsiveness matters more than polished prose during an upstream outage.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A graceful degradation ladder trades conversational polish for deterministic availability across progressive fallback rungs: switch to a secondary model or backup provider first, drop expensive reranking or generation to return cached/extractive snippets from retrieved docs next, fall back to plain BM25 search results if generation fails entirely, and show a clean static retry message as the floor. Immediately jumping to 500 pages users needlessly when retrieval itself still works, while ungrounded parametric fallbacks fabricate product specs. Every degraded rung must display clear UI state (`"Showing matching docs while chat recovers"`) and alert ops so prolonged brownouts never hide silently behind green HTTP 200 metrics.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Retry the primary frontier endpoint 10 times with 5-second waits before failing.
options.why: Ten sequential retries keep threads blocked for 50 seconds and amplify load on a struggling upstream.

options.text: Ask a smaller model to answer without running retrieval.
options.why: Dropping retrieval turns product docs into ungrounded hallucinations.

options.text: Return raw stack traces so power users know which region crashed.
options.why: Exposing internal stack traces hurts UX and leaks topology details.

options.text: Step down a ladder: backup model tier → cached popular answer or fast extractive summary → plain lexical search links → deterministic status message.
options.why: Each rung lowers dependency cost while preserving grounded utility instead of hard-failing.

questions.title: A primary model provider delivers 99.0% availability (0.99), and an independent secondary provider delivers 98.0% availability (0.98). Assuming instant health failover on outage, what is the combined theoretical availability in percent?
questions.context: Assume failure modes across the two providers are statistically independent.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Failover only breaks when **both** providers fail simultaneously: `(1 − 0.99) × (1 − 0.98) = 0.01 × 0.02 = 0.0002` failure probability, yielding combined availability `1 − 0.0002 = 0.9998 = ` **`99.98%`** (cutting downtime by 50× from 7.2 hours/month to ~8.6 minutes/month). In production, shared upstream failures—DNS outages, regional fiber cuts, or identical safety-filter bugs triggered by the same adversarial input—introduce correlation that caps real availability lower than 99.98%. Keeping backups on distinct clouds and testing failover with scheduled chaos drills validates genuine independence at the cost of maintaining dual prompt parity.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Explain the Closed, Open, and Half-Open states of a circuit breaker on an LLM gateway, and clarify why a breaker does not repair a failing model server.
questions.context: Upstream GPU nodes start hanging at 30 s timeouts under load; gateway worker threads are saturating.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A circuit breaker stops callers from piling onto a broken dependency: in **Closed** state, traffic flows normally while tracking rolling error/timeout rates; once failures breach a threshold, it trips **Open** to fail fast locally (or route immediately to fallback) without waiting 30 s per request; after a cooldown timer, it moves to **Half-Open** to admit limited test probes, closing on success or reopening on failure. Without a breaker, 30-second hanging calls exhaust every gateway thread and connection pool, cascading an upstream model stall into a total API outage. Remember that a breaker only buys recovery headroom and protects caller resources—it cannot fix an upstream OOM or bad deploy unless autoscaling, load shedding, or rollback relieves the root cause.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Your LLM gateway's circuit breaker suddenly trips Open during a busy afternoon, dropping healthy requests to a degraded fallback—yet upstream GPU health checks are 100% green. Logs show a surge of `HTTP 400` and guardrail rejection responses from malformed client payloads. What bug triggered the false trip?
questions.context: One enterprise customer deployed a broken script sending oversized invalid JSON payloads for 5 minutes.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Counting `4xx` client mistakes (invalid schemas, auth errors, context-length rejections, or safety blocks) inside the dependency failure counter lets a single buggy client trip the breaker for every healthy tenant. Add **jittered open cooldowns** (`30s ± 10s`), restrict Half-Open probes to **1 in-flight probe per pod** (or coordinate via a central token bucket / slow-start ramp: 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% traffic over 60 seconds), and enforce consecutive successes before closing. questions.title: Under severe upstream GPU saturation, why is strict priority-based load shedding (rejecting background batch jobs first) better than keeping FIFO queues or dropping 20% of all requests at random?

questions.title: During a vector-database timeout on a medical benefits assistant, an engineer suggests falling back to pure LLM generation without context so users still get a fast answer. Why is that dangerous, and what degraded path should you build instead?

Instead, degrade down a **grounded-only ladder**: (1) fall back from vector search to a fast backup BM25/keyword index or precomputed plan-summary cache; (2) if all knowledge stores fail, return a structured deterministic error or link directly to the relevant plan portal section (`"Plan database temporarily unavailable — please verify coverage directly at..."`); and (3) require explicit UI badges on degraded modes. questions.title: Design an automated brownout controller for an enterprise AI research assistant when GPU cluster utilization exceeds 92% or error-budget burn spikes 5×.

questions.title: A tenant's token bucket has a maximum capacity of 120,000 tokens and refills steadily at 2,000 tokens/second (120,000 TPM). Starting from full capacity, a script fires 15 requests consuming 6,000 tokens each immediately, waits 10 seconds, and then fires 10 more requests of 6,000 tokens each (admitted one by one). How many requests in the second wave are rejected with HTTP 429?
questions.context: Assume instantaneous execution within each wave and exact integer token accounting.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Trace the bucket balance step by step:

1. **After wave 1:** `120,000 − (15 × 6,000) = 120,000 − 90,000 = 30,000` tokens left.
2. **After 10 s refill:** `30,000 + (10 × 2,000) = 50,000` tokens available (below the `120,000` cap).
3. **Wave 2 requests:** Each takes `6,000` tokens, so `floor(50,000 ÷ 6,000) = 8` requests are admitted (leaving 2,000 tokens), and `10 − 8 = ` **`2`** requests are rejected with HTTP 429.

Separating burst capacity `B` from sustained refill rate `r` lets operators tighten short-window spikes without lowering a tenant's monthly TPM allowance, though misjudging batch bursts leaves legitimate scripts stalling unless clients respect `Retry-After`.

questions.title: Why do modern LLM providers exempt or heavily discount cached input tokens against Tokens-Per-Minute (TPM) rate limits, and what breaks if your internal gateway fails to mirror that distinction?

Discounting cached reads at ~`0.1×–0.25×` in gateway admission matches true hardware load while requiring post-call header reconciliation.

questions.title: A workflow orchestrator enforces a 400 ms per-call timeout and fans out 12 independent retrieval/scoring calls in parallel per request. Why does p99 end-to-end latency spike far above 400 ms, and how does deadline propagation fix it?

criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.

Pass an absolute **upstream deadline timestamp** (`deadline_ms`) in every RPC header, cancel slower optional fan-out branches once enough results arrive (partial-quorum completion), and forbid inner retries once remaining deadline drops below minimum execution cost. Shared deadlines cap worst-case user wait cleanly at the cost of dropping occasional low-value tail shards.

Enforcing a tight **concurrency / active-token cap** and failing excess requests immediately with `429` + `Retry-After` keeps admitted requests inside SLO and gives clients clean backoff signals (or triggers failover to a secondary cloud API). Fast shedding trades graceful excess refusal for predictable low latency and high goodput on admitted load.

questions.title: Tenant A runs 64k-token PDF summarization jobs while staying strictly inside its 10 RPM limit. Suddenly p99 TTFT for every other tenant sharing the GPU cluster jumps from 220 ms to 4.8 seconds. Why did RPM rate limiting miss this, and what fixes tenant isolation?

questions.title: An engineer adds `user_id` and `prompt_hash` as labels to a Prometheus request counter (`llm_requests_total`), and the metrics backend runs out of memory within hours. Why?

Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.

questions.answer: Metrics engines store an in-memory index entry and chunk buffer for every unique label-set combination: adding unbounded keys like `user_id` or `prompt_hash` across 500 RPS spawns millions of active time-series (`200k users × distinct hashes × buckets`), exhausting RAM and crashing collectors. Keep Prometheus metric labels strictly **low-cardinality** (fewer than ~100 distinct values per label: `model_id`, `route`, `tier`, `status_class`), while emitting `user_id`, `trace_id`, and `prompt_hash` inside **structured JSON logs** and **OpenTelemetry trace attributes** designed for high-cardinality filtering. Separating aggregate metrics from high-cardinality events preserves fast alerting without sacrificing individual-request root-cause debugging.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Prometheus counters cannot increment when strings contain hashes.
options.why: Prometheus accepts arbitrary label strings; the limit is the explosion of distinct label combinations.

options.text: Every unique `(user_id, prompt_hash)` combination creates a permanent new time-series in TSDB memory until retention expires, causing cardinality explosion.
options.why: Time-series databases index every unique label set in RAM; unbounded IDs belong in structured logs or traces.

options.text: High-cardinality labels force Prometheus to disable histogram quantiles.
options.why: Histograms continue computing per series, amplifying cardinality even further (one series per bucket).

options.text: Prometheus scrapes trace spans synchronously inside the HTTP request path.
options.why: Prometheus scrapes `/metrics` asynchronously; the OOM happens inside the time-series index.

questions.title: A faulty prompt change deploys at 14:00, immediately causing silent JSON truncation on 15% of requests. Monitoring alerts page the on-call engineer at 14:12, the bad prompt hash is isolated at 14:28, and a feature-flag rollback restores 100% healthy traffic at 14:39. Measuring MTTR from incident detection (14:12) to full mitigation (14:39), what is MTTR in minutes?
questions.context: Use standard incident lifecycle boundaries: start (14:00), detection (14:12), mitigation (14:39).
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Time from alert detection (`14:12`) to full mitigation (`14:39`) is `39 − 12 = ` **`27`** minutes (`MTTD = 12` minutes; total user-exposure window = `39` minutes). Breaking incidents into detection time (`MTTD`), diagnosis time (`16` min), and execution time (`11` min) pinpoints where reliability investment pays off most: adding real-time schema-failure alerts cuts MTTD from 12 minutes to under 2 minutes, while decoupled prompt-version flags cut rollback time from 11 minutes to seconds without waiting on container rebuilds.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Why are explicit thumbs-up/thumbs-down buttons unreliable as primary production quality telemetry, and which four implicit user signals provide cleaner coverage?
questions.context: Your assistant sees 100,000 daily turns, yet fewer than 1.5% receive an explicit thumbs rating.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Explicit thumbs ratings suffer severe selection and reporting bias—under 2% of users click them, skewing heavily toward outraged edge cases or super-fans while missing silent abandonment on subtle errors. Complement explicit ratings with four high-volume **implicit behavioral signals** logged per `trace_id`: (1) **immediate re-ask / prompt reformulation** within 60 seconds (indicates an unhelpful or missed first reply); (2) **copy / code-insert / action-accept rate** versus discard; (3) **manual undo or edit distance** on AI-drafted text/code; and (4) **human-agent escalation or session drop-off** right after an assistant turn. Implicit signals capture nearly 100% of sessions automatically, at the cost of careful confounding checks (for example, fast session exit can signal either immediate success or total frustration unless paired with copy/click telemetry).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: A production LLM endpoint has a 99.9% monthly availability SLO (allowing a 0.001 error fraction over 30 days). During a 1-hour upstream incident, observed request errors spike to 1.2% (0.012). What is the error-budget burn rate during that hour (as a multiple of the sustainable rate)?
questions.context: Compute burn rate as `observed_error_rate / allowed_error_budget_rate`.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Allowed error rate is `1 − 0.999 = 0.001` (`0.1%`). During the incident, errors run at `0.012 ÷ 0.001 = ` **`12`** × the sustainable budget rate (consuming 12 hours of monthly error budget every single hour, which exhausts the entire 720-hour monthly budget in 60 hours if unmitigated). Expressing severity in burn-rate multiples rather than raw percentages makes alerting consistent across endpoints with different SLOs (99.9% vs 99.99%), while reminding teams to gate non-urgent prompt launches once monthly budget runs low.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: During an incident where users complain of 8-second AI freezes, your Prometheus dashboard using `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)` reports p99 TTFT near `0.95 s`. Yet raw OpenTelemetry traces show 4% of requests taking `7–9 seconds`. What telemetry setup masked the spike?
questions.context: The latency histogram was configured with web-API bucket bounds `[0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, +Inf]`.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Copying default sub-second web-API histogram buckets (`<= 1.0 s`) onto LLM pipelines makes `histogram_quantile` blind to multi-second tail outages. Because Prometheus knows only cumulative bucket counts up to the largest finite edge (`1.0 s`), any spike into `7–9 s` piles indistinguishably into `+Inf` and clamps reported quantiles around `~1.0 s`, leaving dashboards green while users stare at frozen screens. Size LLM histogram buckets logarithmically across actual serving ranges (e.g., `[0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]` seconds for TTFT and full completion, or use DDSketch / native exponential histograms). Wider bucket spans restore accurate p99 visibility at minor extra series overhead (`~10` buckets per route).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: The largest finite bucket ends at `1.0 s`, so 7–9 s LLM requests all fall into `+Inf` and `histogram_quantile` caps or interpolates near the `1.0 s` boundary.
options.why: Prometheus cannot interpolate beyond the top finite bound (`1.0 s`), hiding arbitrary multi-second tail spikes.

options.text: Prometheus histograms drop requests exceeding 5 seconds automatically.
options.why: Observations still increment `+Inf`, which simply lacks resolution above 1.0 s.

options.text: Client-side streaming cancels the metric timer before prefill finishes.
options.why: The traces proved server TTFT actually took 7–9 s.

options.text: `rate()` divides histogram counts by window length, shrinking latencies.
options.why: Ratios inside `histogram_quantile` cancel time denominators.

questions.title: Over a 30-day period, an AI platform team ships 40 distinct releases across prompt templates, retrieval configurations, and model-serving settings. Four releases trigger automated canary rollbacks, two require post-launch hotfix reverts, and one requires an emergency config pin (7 incident-causing releases total). What is the Change Failure Rate (CFR) in percent?
questions.context: Compute CFR across all 40 distinct releases shipped during the month.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Change Failure Rate equals `failed_or_reverted_releases ÷ total_releases = 7 ÷ 40 × 100 = ` **`17.5%`** (nearly one in five changes degraded production enough to require intervention). Tracking CFR separately for prompt/retrieval changes versus serving infrastructure exposes where CI gates are weakest: if 6 of the 7 failures came from unvalidated prompt edits bypassing schema and latency tests, tightening automated pre-merge evals lowers CFR without slowing down deployment frequency.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Over two weeks, user satisfaction drops steadily on long-document queries while HTTP status codes stay 100% 200 OK and p50 latency actually improves slightly. Trace inspection shows prompt + tool schemas grew from 4k to 9k tokens on a server configured with an 8,192-token `max_model_len` and silent truncation. How do you detect and prevent this?
questions.context: New tool definitions and few-shot examples were added gradually across three releases.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Silent prompt truncation drops instructions or retrieved chunks right before generation, making answers fast (shorter inputs) and HTTP-200 clean while quietly lobotomizing accuracy. Prevent silent drops by: (1) rejecting or alerting loudly whenever `prompt_tokens >= 0.90 × model_context_limit` instead of enabling silent left/middle truncation; (2) logging `requested_input_tokens`, `billed_input_tokens`, and `truncation_applied` on every GenAI span; and (3) tracking an **instruction-budget ratio** (`system + tool_schema tokens / max_context`) in CI so schema bloat cannot crowd out user context unnoticed. Explicit truncation errors and context-fill gauges turn multi-week quality decay into immediate actionable alerts, at the cost of handling oversized-input errors cleanly in the client.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Why do production SLO alerting standards use a multi-window, multi-burn-rate rule (for example, triggering a page only when burn rate exceeds 14.4× over BOTH the last 1 hour AND the last 5 minutes) instead of alerting on a single short window or a single static 1% error threshold?
questions.context: Traffic has spiky nightly dips and occasional 30-second client bursts.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A 1-minute error spike resets before an engineer logs in, waking people needlessly, whereas a lone 6-hour rolling alert fires too late and stays firing hours after rollback. Pairing a **long window** (`1 h` at `14.4×` burn rate, confirming meaningful 2% monthly budget loss) with a **short confirmation window** (`5 m` at `14.4×` burn rate, proving the outage is happening *right now*) alerts within ~5 minutes on real severe regressions, ignores 60-second blips, and clears immediately when rollback stops the bleed. Tuning dual windows per SLO tier cuts alert fatigue sharply at the cost of slightly trickier PromQL test validation (`promtool`).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Single-window averages cannot evaluate Prometheus PromQL expressions.
options.why: PromQL supports single windows trivially; the flaw is false-positive noise versus slow detection.

options.text: Multi-window alerts reduce OpenTelemetry span storage by 14.4×.
options.why: Burn-rate rules query aggregated metrics without altering trace sampling retention.

options.text: Static 1% error thresholds only work when traffic exceeds 10,000 QPS.
options.why: Static thresholds fail across both high and low QPS when SLOs differ or brief blips resolve before a human opens a laptop.

options.text: Requiring both a long window (budget impact) and a short window (active failure) catches fast outages quickly, ignores fleeting blips, and auto-resolves promptly once fixed.
options.why: The short window prevents stale pages after mitigation while the long window filters transient noise.

questions.title: After tuning a semantic cache aggressively, aggregate p50 latency drops from 900 ms to 120 ms—yet power users writing novel prompts report 2.4× slower responses than before. Why did aggregate latency metrics lie, and how do you instrument this properly?
questions.context: Cache hit rate jumped to 65%; cold generation now passes through an extra cross-region cache lookup and embedding check.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Because 65% of requests now terminate in 20 ms on cache hits, the **aggregate p50** shifted completely inside the hit population (`120 ms`), masking the fact that the remaining 35% of cache misses slowed from `900 ms` to `2,160 ms` due to extra embedding overhead, lock contention, or GPU cold-cache effects. Bimodal hit/miss latency distributions make global p50 meaningless whenever hit rate moves. Split every latency panel and SLO alert by **`cache_status` (`hit` vs `miss`)** alongside `cache_lookup_ms` overhead, and monitor `miss_p50` and `miss_p99` independently so cache regressions surface immediately. Stratifying by execution path keeps true inference speed honest at the cost of a small bounded `cache_status` label.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What changes in a blameless postmortem when an AI incident stems from probabilistic drift (a subtle prompt edit, upstream model behavior shift, or retrieval index staleness) rather than a deterministic code crash?
questions.context: No server threw an exception; for 3 hours, 22% of financial summaries omitted tax liabilities.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Traditional deterministic postmortems link a commit SHA directly to a stack trace, whereas probabilistic AI incidents require reconstructing exact **data, prompt, and model provenance** to explain why outputs shifted silently. A strong AI postmortem captures: (1) exact immutable `prompt_hash`, `model_snapshot_id`, `retriever_index_version`, and inference parameters (`temperature`, `seed`) at incident time; (2) the **detection gap** explaining why HTTP monitoring missed semantic omissions; (3) **blast-radius quantification** over sampled traces using an offline rubric evaluator; and (4) **durable preventive gates**—promoting failing trace inputs directly into deterministic CI regression tests and adding automated output invariant alerts (e.g., `"tax_field_present_rate"`). Without immutable version tagging across prompts and indexes, teams blame "model flakiness" and repeat the exact outage weeks later.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: At 09:15 UTC, customer escalations spike for wrong invoice totals. API status codes are 100% HTTP 200, GPU utilization looks normal, and no code deploy ran. Walk through the exact triage steps using logs, OpenTelemetry traces, and evaluation telemetry.
questions.context: Your pipeline combines PDF ingestion, hybrid retrieval, and LLM structured extraction.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Follow the causal trace pipeline backward from output to ingestion rather than guessing at prompts:

1. **Correlate by time and slice:** Group recent bad traces by `tenant`, `document_type`, `model_snapshot`, and `index_version` to see if failures hit everything or one upstream change (e.g., an external model update or an overnight ingestion batch).
2. **Inspect LLM inputs vs outputs in traces:** Check whether extracted totals match the retrieved chunks inside the span; if chunks already contain mangled table rows, the fault is **ingestion/parsing**, not the LLM.
3. **Check retrieval score distributions:** Compare `top_k` similarity scores, filter drop counts, and empty-context rates against yesterday's baseline to spot index staleness or embedding drift.
4. **Verify model and guardrail spans:** Check if `model_id` resolved to an updated upstream snapshot, `finish_reason` shifted to `length`, or post-processing normalizers stripped signs/decimals.

Causal trace isolation resolves the right layer in minutes, avoiding wasted prompt rewrites over a broken PDF parser.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Design an OpenTelemetry observability architecture for a 5,000 QPS multi-model AI gateway: specify GenAI span attributes, PII redaction, cost-bounded tail sampling, and real-time incident alerting.
questions.context: Storing 100% of raw traces at 5,000 QPS costs more than GPU inference itself; strict privacy compliance forbids raw PII in central trace stores.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Combine low-cardinality Prometheus metrics at the edge with PII-scrubbed, tail-sampled OpenTelemetry traces. Every gateway and tool step propagates W3C `traceparent` headers and emits OpenTelemetry GenAI attributes (`gen_ai.system`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, `cached_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `prompt_hash`, `finish_reason`, `ttft_ms`, `guardrail_verdict`). Run a local collector processor inside the VPC to mask PII/secrets and store raw prompts only in encrypted short-TTL debug buckets (or drop payloads while retaining hashes and token counts). Use **tail-based sampling** in the collector tier: keep **100%** of traces with `5xx`/`429`, `ttft > SLO`, guardrail triggers, retries, or implicit user re-asks, and keep only **1%–2%** baseline head-sampled healthy traces. Pair edge metrics with multi-window SLO burn alerts and automated token-velocity alarms, giving complete incident visibility at ~5% of full-trace storage cost while requiring sufficient collector buffer RAM for tail-sampling trace assembly.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is a foundation model, and how is it different from a regular ML model?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A single large model pretrained on broad data at massive scale, general-purpose enough to be adapted (via prompting or fine-tuning) to many downstream tasks — instead of one model trained from scratch per task. See [Foundation Model Internals](/docs/llms-genai/foundation-model-internals).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is a Large Language Model, and what is it actually trained to do?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A neural network (almost always a decoder-only Transformer) trained to predict the next token given everything before it. Nothing more exotic than that at the objective level — the wide range of downstream behavior (chat, code, reasoning) emerges from scale plus post-training on top of that one pretraining objective.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is tokenization, and why can't LLMs just read raw text?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Splitting text into a fixed vocabulary of subword units (tokens) the model actually operates on — characters are too fine-grained (long sequences, no semantic unit), whole words are too coarse (unbounded vocabulary, can't handle unseen words). See [Foundation Model Internals — Tokenization](/docs/llms-genai/foundation-model-internals#tokenization).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: A BPE tokenizer meets the rare word "unfathomability". What does it do?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: The algorithm most LLM tokenizers use to build that subword vocabulary: start from individual characters/bytes, and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, until you hit a target vocabulary size. Frequent words end up as one token; rare words fall back to smaller subword pieces.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: It adds the word to the vocabulary on the fly.
options.why: The vocabulary is fixed when the tokenizer is trained.

options.text: It maps the word to a single unknown-word token.
options.why: Byte-level BPE never needs an unknown token: anything can be spelled out from smaller pieces.

options.text: It always splits the word into single characters.
options.why: Only as a last resort. It uses the largest known pieces first.

options.text: It splits the word into smaller subword pieces that are in its vocabulary.
options.why: Frequent words get one token, rare ones fall back to pieces, down to single bytes if needed.

questions.title: What are embeddings?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Dense numeric vectors representing tokens (or whole sentences/documents) such that semantic similarity corresponds to geometric closeness — the representation everything downstream (attention, retrieval) actually operates on. See [Word Embeddings](/docs/nlp/word-embeddings).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Remove positional encoding from a bidirectional (encoder) Transformer. How does it see "dog bites man" versus "man bites dog"?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Self-attention on its own is permutation-invariant — it has no notion of token order. Positional encoding injects order information into the input so the model can tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog." See [Attention & Transformers — Positional Encoding](/docs/deep-learning/attention-transformers#positional-encoding).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Attention weights encode word order on their own.
options.why: Query-key scores depend on content, not position, so they're unchanged when words swap places.

options.text: It still reads left to right, like an RNN.
options.why: There's no recurrence in a Transformer. Order has to be injected.

options.text: It can't tell them apart: each token's representation is the same in both, because self-attention ignores order.
options.why: Without positions, attention treats the input as a set. (A causal mask in a decoder leaks some order information, which is why some decoders cope without explicit positions.)

options.text: Only the first word's position is lost.
options.why: All positions are lost equally.

questions.title: What is self-attention?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: The mechanism letting every token in a sequence look at every other token and weight how much each one matters for updating its own representation — computed from Query/Key/Value projections of the same input. See [Self-Attention: Query, Key, Value](/docs/deep-learning/attention-transformers#self-attention-query-key-value).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What are Query, Key, and Value in attention?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Three learned linear projections of the same input: Query represents "what am I looking for," Key represents "what do I offer" for every other position, and the Query·Key similarity produces attention weights that combine the Values into the output.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: You drop the 1/√d_k scaling from attention in a model with d_k = 128. What goes wrong first?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Without scaling, dot products grow large as the key dimension grows, pushing softmax into a region with near-zero gradients (it saturates toward one-hot). Dividing by √d_k keeps the scores in a range where softmax stays well-behaved. See [Why Scale by the Square Root of the Key Dimension](/docs/deep-learning/attention-transformers#why-scale-by-the-square-root-of-the-key-dimension).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Nothing, because softmax normalises any scale.
options.why: Softmax normalises the sum, not the sharpness. Multiplying every score by 10 changes the output a lot.

options.text: Scores grow with the dimension, softmax saturates towards one-hot, and gradients through it nearly vanish.
options.why: Dividing by √d_k keeps the scores' variance near 1 whatever the dimension.

options.text: Memory use grows.
options.why: The scale factor doesn't change any tensor's size.

options.text: Attention becomes uniform across tokens.
options.why: The opposite: large scores make attention peakier, not flatter.

questions.title: What is multi-head attention, and why not just use one big attention head?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Running several smaller attention computations in parallel, each with its own learned projections, then concatenating the results — letting different heads specialize in different kinds of relationships (syntax, coreference, position) instead of one head averaging everything together. See [Multi-Head Attention](/docs/deep-learning/attention-transformers#multi-head-attention).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: In an encoder-decoder translation model, where do the queries, keys and values in the decoder's cross-attention come from?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Self-attention: Query, Key, and Value all come from the same sequence. Cross-attention: Query comes from one sequence (e.g. a decoder), Key and Value come from a different one (e.g. an encoder's output) — how an encoder-decoder model lets its decoder attend to the source input. See [Cross-Attention](/docs/deep-learning/attention-transformers#cross-attention).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder's output.
options.why: The decoder asks the questions, and the source sentence supplies the answers.

options.text: All three from the decoder.
options.why: That's the decoder's self-attention, which is a separate layer.

options.text: Queries from the encoder, keys and values from the decoder.
options.why: That's reversed.

options.text: All three from the encoder.
options.why: Then the decoder's own state would play no part.

questions.title: Someone trains a decoder-only language model and forgets the causal mask. Training loss drops unusually fast. What happens at generation time?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Causal masking blocks a position from attending to future positions, which is what makes autoregressive next-token generation well-defined — without it, predicting token *n* could see token *n+1*, which doesn't exist at inference time. See [Masking](/docs/deep-learning/attention-transformers#masking).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: It can no longer produce text of any kind.
options.why: It still produces tokens. They're just poor, because training taught it the wrong task.

options.text: It generates better, because it saw more context in training.
options.why: It saw context that doesn't exist at inference time, so what it learned doesn't transfer.

options.text: Nothing changes, because masking only matters during inference.
options.why: The mask matters most during training, where every position is predicted in parallel.

options.text: It fails: in training it could see the next token, so it learned to copy instead of predict.
options.why: The suspiciously fast loss drop is the giveaway. At generation time, there is no next token to copy.

questions.title: A model has 24 layers and 16 key-value heads of dimension 64, and stores the cache in fp16. How much KV cache does each token add? (KiB.)
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
Keys and values, for every layer and KV head: 2 × 24 × 16 × 64 × 2 bytes = 98,304 bytes = **96 KiB** per token. A 4,000-token conversation needs about 375 MiB for one user.

Storing each generated token's Key/Value projections so they don't get recomputed on every subsequent step — without it, generating token *n* would redo the attention computation for all *n-1* prior tokens from scratch. It's also the dominant consumer of GPU memory during serving, which is why techniques like GQA/MQA exist to shrink it. See [KV Cache](/docs/llms-genai/foundation-model-internals#kv-cache).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Your assistant must quote from a 50,000-item price list that changes every day. Fine-tune, or retrieve?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Retrieving relevant documents at query time and feeding them into the model's context alongside the question, rather than baking that knowledge into the weights. Fine-tuning is slow to update, doesn't cite sources, and doesn't scale to knowledge that changes daily — RAG updates by re-indexing, not retraining. See [RAG](/docs/llms-genai/rag).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Retrieve it at query time (RAG), so answers always use today's prices.
options.why: Facts that change daily belong in an index you update, not in model weights.

options.text: Fine-tune once and refresh it monthly.
options.why: Prices would be wrong for most of each month.

options.text: Fine-tune every night.
options.why: Slow and expensive, unreliable at reproducing exact figures, and it can't cite where a price came from.

options.text: Paste the whole price list into the system prompt.
options.why: Not for 50,000 items: far too many tokens on every request.

questions.title: What are the main stages of a RAG pipeline?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Chunk the source documents, embed each chunk, index the embeddings in a vector store, embed the incoming query, retrieve the nearest chunks, then feed those chunks plus the query into the LLM as context. See [The RAG Pipeline, End to End](/docs/llms-genai/rag#the-rag-pipeline-end-to-end).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Your chunks are 2,000 tokens. Answers cite the right document but miss the specific clause asked about. What's the likely chunking problem?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Splitting source documents into retrievable pieces. Too small and a chunk loses surrounding context needed to make sense of it; too large and irrelevant content dilutes the embedding, hurting retrieval precision, and wastes context budget once retrieved. See [Chunking Strategies](/docs/llms-genai/rag#chunking-strategies).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: The embedding model is too large.
options.why: Model size doesn't cause dilution inside a chunk.

options.text: The chunks are too big: the clause is a small part of each chunk, so its signal in the embedding is diluted.
options.why: Smaller chunks, or splitting on section boundaries, give the clause its own embedding.

options.text: The chunks are too small.
options.why: Small chunks lose context, but the symptom here is the right document without the right detail, which points the other way.

options.text: Top-k is too low.
options.why: The right document is already being retrieved. It's the detail inside it that's lost.

questions.title: Users search for the error code "E-4012". Dense retrieval returns pages about errors in general, never the one page about E-4012. What helps most?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Dense retrieval compares learned embedding vectors by semantic similarity — catches paraphrases and synonyms, misses exact rare terms. Sparse retrieval (BM25) matches on literal term overlap — exact on keywords/IDs/jargon, blind to synonyms. See [Dense vs. Sparse Retrieval, and BM25](/docs/llms-genai/rag#dense-vs-sparse-retrieval-and-bm25).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Raise top-k.
options.why: The right page may not be among the dense candidates at all.

options.text: Add keyword retrieval (BM25) alongside dense retrieval, and merge the two (hybrid search).
options.why: Exact rare tokens like error codes are what sparse retrieval is good at.

options.text: Rewrite the query with an LLM first.
options.why: Rewriting doesn't tell the retriever which page contains the code.

options.text: Use a bigger embedding model.
options.why: Rare identifiers are poorly represented in embeddings whatever the model size.

questions.title: What is BM25?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A classical sparse-retrieval ranking function scoring documents by term-frequency overlap with the query, with diminishing returns for repeated terms and normalization for document length — no learning, no embeddings, still a strong, fast baseline decades later.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: With reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60), a document ranks 1st in the dense results and 3rd in the sparse results. What's its fused score? (Four decimals.)
