questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: The KV cache of the shared system prompt.
options.why: That's exactly what prompt caching is for.

options.text: Answers personalised to the user's own account or permissions.
options.why: One user's answer is wrong, or a leak, for another.

options.text: FAQ answers keyed by document version.
options.why: With the version in the key, they're fresh by construction.

options.text: Embeddings of documents that never change.
options.why: Safe to cache indefinitely.

questions.title: What's a production “router + fallback” pattern for a RAG system, and what should the router itself cost?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A practical router has three parts: a rule-based pre-filter for deterministic cases (explicit entity codes route to an exact-match path, greetings route to a cached response), a lightweight classifier for genuine semantic intent classification on everything else, and confidence-based promotion — even if the router initially classifies a query as simple, if the retrieved results score poorly, it falls through to a more thorough tier automatically rather than returning a weak answer. The router itself should stay cheap and fast (under roughly 50ms added latency, a tiny fraction of a cent per call) to remain a net positive; track tier distribution as an ongoing KPI, since a creeping share of traffic landing in the expensive tier can mean either the router is miscategorizing or the real query mix has genuinely shifted.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What's the fan-out/fan-in pattern in RAG, and what's RAG-Fusion a special case of?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Multiple retrieval strategies (or query reformulations, or retrievers over different sub-corpora) run in parallel — fanning out — and their results get merged into one ranked list — fanning in — typically via Reciprocal Rank Fusion since it handles differently-scaled result lists without needing score calibration. RAG-Fusion is exactly this pattern specialized to one specific fan-out source: multiple LLM-generated rephrasings of the same query, rather than multiple genuinely different retrieval strategies or sub-corpora.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: RAG in Production — Monitoring, Debugging & Incidents
questions.title: What is “conversational context drift” as a distinct failure mode, and how do you detect it before it causes a bad answer?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: It's specifically when a multi-turn system's retrieval degrades because a follow-up query has lost the context that made it meaningful, as opposed to a single-turn retrieval failure which has nothing to do with conversation history at all. Detect it proactively by monitoring the similarity between a condensed/rewritten follow-up query and the raw retrieval results it produces — a sharp drop in retrieved-result relevance scores right after a topic-shift-shaped follow-up is a strong leading indicator, worth catching before it ever reaches a visibly wrong answer.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: RAG in Production — Monitoring, Debugging & Incidents
questions.title: Your RAG system's p99 latency just doubled with no obvious deploy. How do you debug it?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Localize before you guess: check whether it's a specific pipeline stage (a slow vector DB index after a cold start or node change, a reranker that started receiving a larger-than-usual candidate set, a prompt-caching cache-miss spike from a prefix that stopped matching) versus a traffic-mix shift (a sudden influx of queries that route to a more expensive tier or trigger more retrieval hops). Pull per-stage latency from your traces rather than only looking at end-to-end p99 — "it got slower" isn't actionable, "retrieval p99 tripled specifically" is.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Add a cache.
options.why: That might hide the symptom without finding the cause.

options.text: Break p99 down by pipeline stage from traces, and check whether the traffic mix shifted.
options.why: "It's slower" isn't actionable. "Retrieval p99 tripled" is.

options.text: Move to a faster LLM.
options.why: That's a guess at the stage.

options.text: Roll back the latest deploy.
options.why: There wasn't one.

questions.section: RAG in Production — Monitoring, Debugging & Incidents
questions.title: What's the real difference between retrieval failure's observable symptoms and its root causes, and why does that distinction matter for debugging?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Symptoms are what users or monitoring actually see — irrelevant answers, "I don't know" responses, low confidence scores; root causes are what actually produced them — embedding-space mismatch between query and document vocabulary (the semantic gap problem), a chunking strategy that split the relevant fact across a boundary, a stale index missing recently-added content, or a mis-tuned top-k. The distinction matters because the same symptom can have several different root causes, and the fix for each is completely different — treating a symptom (e.g. "just add more context") without finding the actual root cause routinely makes things worse, not better.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: RAG in Production — Monitoring, Debugging & Incidents
questions.title: What's cascading retrieval failure, and how is it different from a single, isolated retrieval miss?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: It's when one technique's failure actively propagates and amplifies through the rest of the pipeline rather than staying contained — the canonical example is HyDE: if the generated hypothetical document is itself subtly wrong, the system doesn't just fail to retrieve the best chunk, it confidently retrieves chunks relevant to the *wrong* hypothetical, which can look more convincing (and be harder to catch) than a normal low-relevance-score miss. In multi-hop RAG the same shape shows up as a wrong intermediate fact at hop one actively steering every subsequent hop further from the correct answer, rather than each hop failing independently.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: RAG in Production — Monitoring, Debugging & Incidents
questions.title: What's a stale index problem in production, and what's the actual fix — beyond “just re-index more often”?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A naive fix (more frequent full rebuilds) doesn't scale and still leaves a staleness window between rebuilds. The real fix is detecting exactly which documents changed — via a content hash or modification timestamp tracked per source document — and re-embedding only those, incrementally, continuously, rather than paying the cost and staleness window of a periodic full rebuild. Also worth naming explicitly: staleness interacts with other failure modes, since a stale index can produce a confident, well-formed, entirely outdated answer that looks indistinguishable from a correct one until someone checks the document's actual current version.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: RAG in Production — Monitoring, Debugging & Incidents
questions.title: What causes embedding mismatch in production, and what are its observable symptoms?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Root causes span several dimensions: a domain shift the original embedding model was never trained for, a language the model has weak coverage of, an architecture change when swapping embedding models without fully re-embedding the existing index (leaving old and new vectors geometrically incompatible in the same store), or simple model-version drift over time. The symptom is usually subtle rather than catastrophic — retrieval quality silently degrades in a way that looks like "the model got worse at understanding queries" when it's actually a mismatch between how the query and the stored documents were embedded, not a quality regression in either encoder individually.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Why does simple input sanitization fail as a defense against prompt injection in RAG, and why does hardening the system prompt also fail?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Sanitization fails because an attacker can rephrase malicious instructions in countless ways that never match a fixed filter pattern — "ignore previous instructions" gets blocked, but a thousand semantically-equivalent rewordings don't. System-prompt hardening fails for a more structural reason: when a retrieved document contains conflicting instructions, the model has no principled way to always weight the older, more abstract system prompt over the more recent, more specific instruction sitting right in its context — in practice, the more recent and specific instruction often wins, regardless of which one the system intended to be authoritative.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What does an actual defense-in-depth strategy against prompt injection in a RAG system look like, given no single defense fully solves it?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Layer multiple partial defenses rather than relying on one: structural separation (clearly delimit retrieved content from trusted instructions, e.g. with XML-style tags the model is prompted to treat context as data, never as commands), content filtering at ingestion (flag documents containing injection-like patterns without necessarily auto-blocking them, since false positives on legitimate content are a real cost), sandboxed extraction for any document-processing step that itself executes code or fetches further content, output inspection for signs an injection succeeded, and privilege separation so even a successful injection can't take an action beyond what that specific context should ever be allowed to do. The honest framing for an interview: this raises the cost and reduces the success rate of an attack, it does not eliminate the risk — claiming a "solved" defense is itself a red flag in an answer.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Design a RAG system over SharePoint-style documents that must respect existing, possibly-changing document permissions. Walk through it.
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Seven steps, in order: clarify requirements first (single org or multi-tenant, how fresh must permission checks be — minutes or seconds, what scale of users/groups); ingestion via a connector that produces chunks plus embeddings plus resolved per-chunk ACL metadata; identity resolution where the user's group memberships get expanded at query time and cached with a short TTL; retrieval that pre-filters *inside* the ANN search itself on tenant and permission match, not after; a late-binding permission re-check against the authoritative source on the final top-k right before generation, failing closed on any gap; permission-awareness extended beyond retrieval itself (ACL-aware citations, permission-scoped cache keys, a zero-retention LLM endpoint); and an audit layer logging user, applied filter, and chunk IDs per query, plus periodic cross-tenant probe tests. Naming the two-gate model explicitly — a cheap metadata pre-filter plus an authoritative late-binding check — and the staleness window between them is what distinguishes a senior answer from "just add a metadata filter."
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Retrieval is correctly filtered by permissions. Then a "related documents" feature follows links from the retrieved chunks to other documents. What's the risk?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Any stage added after the ACL gate that touches document content can reintroduce a leak even though retrieval itself was correctly filtered — a reranker that re-queries the index for more candidates without reapplying the filter, a semantic cache that returns an answer generated under a different, broader-permission user's session, a "related documents" link-expansion step that follows references from an authorized chunk into an unauthorized one, or a summarization-memory layer that condensed an earlier, more-privileged session into context reused later. The principle worth stating explicitly: authorization has to be enforced at the *last* point document content enters the prompt, and every component between retrieval and generation has to be either ACL-aware itself or provably content-blind.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Lower recall.
options.why: If anything it adds documents.

options.text: It can pull in documents the user isn't allowed to see, because it runs after the permission filter.
options.why: Every stage that adds content after the filter has to be permission-aware itself.

options.text: Answers get slower.
options.why: A real cost, but not the risk that matters here.

options.text: Duplicate chunks.
options.why: A quality nuisance, not a breach.

questions.title: Why is filtering the LLM's output for restricted content the wrong place to enforce access control, versus filtering what gets retrieved?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: By the time restricted content reaches the model it has already crossed the trust boundary — it may be logged or retained by the model provider regardless of what the final visible output ends up saying. Output filtering also depends on correctly recognizing and stripping every possible leak after the fact (often via a second LLM-as-guard), and that detection step is bypassable the same way any LLM behavior is bypassable. Filter what goes in — what gets retrieved — not what comes out.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: An approximate search returns the top 100 candidates, then a permission filter keeps only documents this user may see: 2% of the corpus. If permissions are unrelated to relevance, how many results are left on average?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
100 × 0.02 = **2** results, and often zero. Filtering after an approximate top-k throws away almost everything for users who can see little. That's why the fix is to filter during the search, or partition by permission.

When a user can legitimately see only a tiny slice of the corpus, HNSW's greedy graph traversal can get stranded in regions where almost no node satisfies the filter, since most of the graph's edges lead toward ineligible vectors the traversal has no reason to route around. Fixes: use a filterable-graph engine that builds extra links specifically to keep filtered traversal connected, fall back to brute-force scan below some match-ratio threshold where approximate search would otherwise fail, or move to per-tenant/per-permission-class index partitions so the permission boundary *is* the partition boundary rather than a predicate layered awkwardly on top of one shared graph.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What's the security risk of semantic caching specifically in a multi-tenant RAG system, beyond the obvious “wrong answer served”?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Beyond a naive cross-tenant leak (Tenant A's cached answer served to Tenant B's semantically-similar query), there are two subtler ones: a timing side-channel, where a cache hit (fast) versus a cache miss (slow) lets one tenant infer whether another tenant has previously queried a given topic, purely from response latency; and document-ID leakage in cache metadata, where an implementation that caches retrieved chunk IDs alongside the answer exposes *which documents are relevant to a topic* even if the answer text itself is withheld. The fix for all three is the same: namespace every cache key by tenant/user ID and include a hash of the current permission set in the key, not just the query embedding.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: How do you handle a real-time permission change — a user loses access to a document mid-session — so a cached or in-flight answer doesn't leak it?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Three layers together: a short TTL on any cached permission data (5–60 seconds for sensitive data, with every cache read checking freshness against the TTL); a late-binding check on the final top-k that re-verifies the user's *current* permissions against the authoritative source right before generation, not against stale index metadata; and session/cache invalidation triggered by the permission-change event itself — when a revocation fires, invalidate active sessions that may hold a cached answer referencing the now-revoked document, and flush any semantic-cache entries whose source documents include it. Combined, this means a user who loses access mid-session gets blocked at their *next* query, not left holding a stale cached answer indefinitely.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: How does tenant offboarding differ between a structurally-isolated deployment and a shared-index-with-filter deployment?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Structural isolation (a separate namespace, index, or cluster per tenant) makes offboarding trivial — drop the tenant's namespace or index, which doubles as a clean, demonstrable answer to a right-to-erasure request. A shared index requires a delete-by-filter pass across every chunk belonging to that tenant, plus real verification that the vectors are actually gone from both the live index *and* any backups or snapshots — an operation that's genuinely easy to get subtly wrong (partial deletes, lingering tombstones in the HNSW graph, or backups quietly retaining vectors the live system reports as deleted).
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Design a RAG system for a legal document corpus where different law firms share the platform but must never see each other's documents, and every answer must cite its exact source.
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Requirements first: strict per-tenant isolation (structural, not filter-based, given the sensitivity), citation at the passage level since legal answers are worthless without exact attribution, and an audit trail since this is a compliance-sensitive domain. Architecture: per-tenant index partitions (not a shared index with a filter — the stakes are too high for the HNSW-recall and leakage risks a shared index introduces), citation enforced via NLI-checked attribution at generation time rather than trusted model-reported citations, a late-binding permission check even within a single firm's own multi-user access tiers, and per-query audit logging of user, filter applied, and chunk IDs retrieved. The interview signal here is naming the isolation-model tradeoff explicitly (structural vs. shared-plus-filter) and justifying it against this specific domain's stakes, not defaulting to whichever is cheaper.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Your RAG system's answer quality has been stable for months, then degrades sharply this week with no deploy. Walk through your investigation.
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Check, roughly in this order of likelihood and cheapness-to-check: has the source corpus itself changed in a way that broke a downstream assumption (a new document format, a schema change in an ingested database); has the embedding or generation model been silently updated on the provider side (providers do this without always announcing it clearly); has traffic mix shifted (a new, harder query distribution rather than an actual system regression); and has the index gone stale or partially corrupted (a failed incremental update left it partially out of sync). The point of the answer isn't getting the exact cause right blind — it's demonstrating a systematic elimination process rather than guessing at a fix and hoping.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: How would you migrate a production RAG system to a new embedding model with zero user-facing downtime?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Blue/green, never in-place: build the new index fully from the new embedding model alongside the still-serving old index, verify the new index's quality against your golden set before any traffic touches it, then cut over atomically once validated — never partially update one index with a mix of old and new vectors, since they live in geometrically incompatible spaces and mixing them silently corrupts every similarity score involving one of each. Handle the migration window explicitly too: any document ingested while the rebuild is in progress needs to be embedded with *both* models (or the cutover needs to be fast enough that the window is negligible), or it risks landing in the wrong index with the wrong embedding version.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Take the service down overnight and rebuild.
options.why: That's downtime, which is what the question rules out.

options.text: Re-embed documents in place, a batch at a time.
options.why: During the migration the index mixes incompatible vectors, and similarity scores become meaningless.

options.text: Switch the query embeddings first, then the documents.
options.why: Every query would be compared against vectors from a different model.

options.text: Blue/green: build a full new index with the new model beside the old one, validate it, then switch over at once.
options.why: Old and new vectors must never share an index.

questions.title: When would you choose Cache-Augmented Generation over RAG for a given use case, as an actual design decision rather than a trivia question?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: CAG makes sense specifically when the corpus is small enough to fully fit in a model's KV cache budget and is relatively stable — a single product manual, a fixed set of policy documents — because it sidesteps every retrieval-quality failure mode by construction (there's no "wrong chunk retrieved" if nothing was ever selectively retrieved at all). It stops making sense the moment the corpus grows past the cache budget, updates frequently enough that cache invalidation becomes constant, or genuinely needs to scale beyond what any single context window can hold — at which point you're back to standard RAG, or a hybrid where a stable core knowledge base is cached and a fast-changing slice is retrieved.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: How would you design retrieval for a corpus that will eventually reach billions of documents, from the start, without having to re-architect later?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A two-tier retrieval architecture from day one, even if the corpus is small initially: coarse retrieval combining BM25 (which scales to any corpus size via an inverted index) with quantized dense embeddings to pull a few thousand candidates from the full corpus cheaply, followed by a precise reranking pass (cross-encoder or ColBERT) over just that narrowed candidate set. Partition the index by a natural dimension (topic, date, document type) from the start so sharding is a configuration change later, not a rewrite — retrofitting partitioning onto a system designed as one flat index is far more painful than building it in from the first version.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: A stakeholder asks “why don't we just fine-tune the model on all our documents instead of building RAG?” How do you answer that in an interview setting?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Walk through the real tradeoffs rather than just asserting RAG is better: fine-tuning bakes facts into weights, which means every single update to the knowledge base requires retraining — infeasible for anything that changes daily or weekly; fine-tuning also can't cite sources, since facts get blended into the weights with no traceable provenance back to a specific document, which matters enormously for trust and auditability; and fine-tuning on a large, diverse document set is actually quite data- and compute-expensive relative to RAG's "re-index the new document" update cost. RAG's answer to the same stakeholder: it updates by re-indexing, not retraining, it can cite its sources, and it scales to more documents than you'd ever want to fit into a single fine-tuning run — fine-tuning still has its place (tone, format, a narrow skill), just not as a substitute for keeping facts current.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: Ten instances run at 60% peak utilization across zones of four, three, and three. Is losing one zone safe?
questions.title: Ten instances run at 60% peak utilization across zones of four, three, and three. Is losing one zone safe?
questions.context: Peak traffic is 6,000 requests/s; each instance safely serves 1,000 requests/s. Failure utilization must remain at or below 70%.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Ten instances are insufficient for the stated failure target. Losing the largest zone leaves six instances at 100% utilization. Fourteen instances placed five, five, and four leave nine survivors at 66.7%. This assumes even routing and the tested per-instance capacity remains valid under failure; the database and routing layer must survive too.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: A worker autoscaler finally matches arrival rate, but queue age keeps rising. What do you inspect?
questions.title: A worker autoscaler finally matches arrival rate, but queue age keeps rising. What do you inspect?
questions.context: Arrivals are 6,000 jobs/s. Capacity was 4,000/s for ninety seconds and is now 6,000/s.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: The fleet accumulated 180,000 jobs during startup. Matching arrivals stops queue growth but does not drain existing backlog, so old jobs remain delayed. At 8,000 completions/s, spare capacity is 2,000/s and takes ninety seconds to drain that backlog under steady arrivals. Inspect actual completions, oldest-job age, dependency saturation, and retry traffic before adding workers.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: A user saves a change and immediately sees the old value. How do you restore a session guarantee?
questions.title: A user saves a change and immediately sees the old value. How do you restore a session guarantee?
questions.context: The primary acknowledged version eight; an asynchronous replica still serves version seven.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Route the session read to the primary or carry a minimum version barrier and wait for a replica that has applied version eight. More replicas alone do not guarantee read-your-writes. Bound waiting by the request deadline and define primary fallback or an explicit failure. Continue using weaker replica reads for operations where that staleness is acceptable.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: Two buyers each reserve six of ten remaining items. How do you prevent overselling?
questions.title: Two buyers each reserve six of ten remaining items. How do you prevent overselling?
questions.context: Both requests may read the same initial stock. The invariant is that confirmed remaining inventory cannot be negative.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Use an atomic conditional decrement that updates only when available stock is at least six, and check whether a row was updated. Alternatively use a correctly scoped transaction with locking or serializable isolation and whole-transaction retry. A separate read followed by an unconditional computed write can accept twelve units. Keep the inventory authority within the transaction boundary.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: A worker commits an effect and crashes before acknowledging the event. What should redelivery do?
questions.title: A worker commits an effect and crashes before acknowledging the event. What should redelivery do?
questions.context: The broker provides at-least-once delivery. The effect is a database update owned by the consumer.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Redelivery should look up a stable event identity recorded atomically with the business update. If it exists, skip the effect and acknowledge; if not, apply the update and insert the identity in one transaction. A process-local set disappears on restart. This protects the database effect, not an unrelated external provider call outside that transaction.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: A paused lock holder resumes after its lease expired and a new holder started. What prevents corruption?
questions.title: A paused lock holder resumes after its lease expired and a new holder started. What prevents corruption?
questions.context: The old holder has token 41; the replacement has token 42. Both can still reach the protected store.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: The protected store must atomically reject writes with an older fencing token after accepting token 42. Lease expiry lets a replacement acquire authority but cannot stop old code from running. Persist the accepted authority at the resource and consider per-owner sequencing for repeated writes. Shortening lease time alone does not solve the stale writer problem.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: An order commits but its publication event disappears after a crash. How do you close the gap?
questions.title: An order commits but its publication event disappears after a crash. How do you close the gap?
questions.context: The order database and broker do not share a transaction. Consumers tolerate at-least-once delivery.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Write the order and an outbox row in one local transaction, then let a relay publish committed rows. A relay crash after publication can duplicate the event, so preserve the event identity and deduplicate consumers. Monitor oldest unpublished age and support replay. Publishing before the database commit only changes the failure into an event for an uncommitted order.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: Three synchronous replicas all received an accidental delete. What recovery evidence do you need?
questions.title: Three synchronous replicas all received an accidental delete. What recovery evidence do you need?
questions.context: The latest recoverable backup is fifteen minutes old. Detection takes five minutes, restore forty, and validation five.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Replicas alone cannot undo the delete; restore a retained backup or recoverable historical point. The modeled potential data gap is fifteen minutes and recovery time is fifty minutes. Test restoration with disaster-time permissions, keys, log replay, and application validation. A successful backup job does not prove those objectives are met.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: A short-link revocation races with a slow cache fill. How do you preserve the deletion deadline?
questions.title: A short-link revocation races with a slow cache fill. How do you preserve the deletion deadline?
questions.context: A reader fetched destination version seven; revocation wrote tombstone version eight before the reader fills the cache.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Prevent version seven from replacing the newer tombstone through a version-aware cache write or an equivalent proven invalidation protocol. Bound every cache lifetime within the revocation contract, including edge and client policies. A simple delete can race with an old refill. If clients retain permanent redirects indefinitely, the service cannot promise immediate revocation through those copies.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: Ten gateways each give one tenant a local burst of five. Is the global burst five?
questions.title: Ten gateways each give one tenant a local burst of five. Is the global burst five?
questions.context: Each local bucket refills at two requests/s. The intended global policy is burst five and sustained two/s.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: No. Independent buckets permit a combined burst of fifty and sustained rate twenty/s. Use one atomic owner per key, or partition leased allowance so the total and failover overshoot are explicitly bounded. Specify fail-open, fail-closed, or bounded fallback by operation risk. A store timeout is different from a known quota rejection.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: A celebrity post cannot finish fan-out before the freshness target. How do you redesign the feed?
questions.title: A celebrity post cannot finish fan-out before the freshness target. How do you redesign the feed?
questions.context: The author has ten million followers; dedicated fan-out capacity is 50,000 inbox inserts/s, and freshness target is five seconds.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Fan-out alone takes two hundred seconds, so use a hybrid feed: precompute ordinary-author inboxes and merge high-fan-out author posts at read time. Deduplicate references and use stable cursor ordering. Recheck current visibility rather than trusting copied inbox data. The trade-off is lower write amplification against greater read-time fan-in.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: A sender retries after its chat acknowledgment disappears. How do you avoid a second message?
questions.title: A sender retries after its chat acknowledgment disappears. How do you avoid a second message?
questions.context: The first attempt committed conversation sequence 418. The socket closed before the sender saw acceptance.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Retry with the same client message ID. The conversation owner atomically maps that identity to the already committed sequence 418 and returns it. A reconnecting receiver resumes after its durable conversation cursor and deduplicates live overlap. Durable acceptance, device delivery, and read receipts are separate states.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: A notification provider times out after accepting a send. Should another provider send immediately?
questions.title: A notification provider times out after accepting a send. Should another provider send immediately?
questions.context: The first provider may have accepted the message; the notification has a stable intent identity and an expiry.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Preserve an unknown outcome and reconcile through the original provider identity or status API before another irreversible send. Immediate failover can duplicate delivery. Keep provider acceptance separate from device delivery, enforce expiry and current preferences, and document the duplicate-versus-loss policy when the provider cannot deduplicate or report status.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: One million viewers average 4 Mb/s each. What does a 95% CDN byte-hit rate leave at origin?
questions.title: One million viewers average 4 Mb/s each. What does a 95% CDN byte-hit rate leave at origin?
questions.context: Use decimal units and separate media bandwidth from playback API request rate.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Delivery is 4 Tb/s, or 500 GB/s. At a 95% byte-hit rate, origin still serves 25 GB/s. Size origin and shielding for cold-cache and purge scenarios, and distinguish request-hit rate from byte-hit rate. Publish a playable manifest only after required segments validate; CDN capacity cannot repair missing source objects.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: An older autocomplete request completes last. How do you keep results correct?
questions.title: An older autocomplete request completes last. How do you keep results correct?
questions.context: The request for ca has generation eight; cat has generation nine. Popularity refreshes hourly but blocked terms must disappear sooner.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Render only the response whose generation matches the current input. Cancellation helps resource use but does not replace this check. Serve a coherent versioned candidate index and apply current suppression separately so blocking does not wait for a full popularity rebuild. Avoid exposing rare private query strings as public suggestions.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: Two matchers choose the same driver from a stale location index. Who decides the winner?
questions.title: Two matchers choose the same driver from a stale location index. Who decides the winner?
questions.context: Location reports arrive every five seconds; exclusive assignment is mandatory even when discovery is stale.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: The authoritative driver or trip store decides through an atomic conditional reservation. Both matchers can discover the driver, but only one can transition the expected available version to offered. The loser chooses another candidate. Offer acceptance and expiry must also check identity and version so delayed work cannot replace newer state.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: A charge may have succeeded but the provider response was lost. What does the payment API return?
questions.title: A charge may have succeeded but the provider response was lost. What does the payment API return?
questions.context: The request has customer-scoped key k17 and amount 1,000 cents. Ledger and provider are separate authorities.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Return the durable operation identity with pending or unknown status until provider evidence resolves it. Reuse the supported provider idempotency identity and reject a different amount under k17. Post balanced ledger entries once under a unique operation constraint when the accounting event is established. Reconcile provider reports and verified callbacks; a timeout does not authorize another charge.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.section: A file upload finishes its chunks but loses the metadata version race. What should readers see?
questions.title: A file upload finishes its chunks but loses the metadata version race. What should readers see?
questions.context: File manifests are immutable; the current pointer is changed conditionally after chunk durability acknowledgments.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Readers keep seeing the previous complete version because the conditional manifest commit failed. Uploaded chunks remain unpublished orphans until safe garbage collection accounts for active uploads and retained versions. Verify hashes on reads and repair lost copies across failure domains. Replica count alone does not prove recovery or corruption detection.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?
